structuralShifts.title: The product moved from model to system
structuralShifts.description: In 2021 the salient artifact was a checkpoint. By 2026 the useful unit was a routed model family plus tools, memory, retrieval, computer access, sandboxes, compaction, identity, review, and durable execution.

structuralShifts.title: Post-training became a primary frontier
structuralShifts.description: InstructGPT, RLHF, constitutional AI, direct preference methods, verifiable-reward RL, tool-use training, self-verification, and environment-based agent RL repeatedly changed usefulness without proportional changes in pretraining scale.

structuralShifts.title: Inference compute became adjustable
structuralShifts.description: Reasoning modes, effort controls, parallel branches, swarms, Heavy/Ultra tiers, and specialist subagents let products spend more compute after the prompt. “Model size” alone stopped describing delivered intelligence.

structuralShifts.title: Open weights became a geopolitical distribution channel
structuralShifts.description: Llama created the mass ecosystem; Mistral, Qwen, DeepSeek, GLM, and Kimi made it globally competitive. Open distribution spread capability and weakened API pricing power, even when training data and full recipes stayed closed.

structuralShifts.title: Coding was the bridge to general agency
structuralShifts.description: Copilot proved commercial demand; ReAct supplied a pattern; AutoGPT exposed failure modes; Cursor, Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Devin, and Grok Build turned repository and terminal work into a proving ground for planning, tools, verification, and long-run state.

structuralShifts.title: The AI chip became an AI factory
structuralShifts.description: H100 scarcity first privileged the accelerator. Blackwell/Rubin, Ultra Ethernet, NVLink, optics, custom ASICs, wafer-scale engines, and rack-level cooling shifted value toward the entire powered and networked system. TSMC and advanced packaging remained beneath nearly every path.

structuralShifts.title: Latency re-entered the capability equation
structuralShifts.description: Groq, Cerebras, Taalas, speculative decoding, sparse attention, and model tiers showed that a slightly weaker instant model—or the same frontier model served 10–14× faster—could enable a qualitatively different product.

structuralShifts.title: Governance moved inside the release architecture
structuralShifts.description: The EU AI Act, executive orders, export controls, safety institutes, frontier-safety laws, copyright cases, and restricted cyber variants affected who could train, access, document, or deploy a system. Policy was no longer an external afterthought.

events.title: OpenAI releases CLIP and previews DALL·E
events.development: OpenAI paired the contrastive vision-language model CLIP with DALL·E, a 12-billion-parameter GPT-3 variant that generated images from captions.
events.technicalChange: CLIP learned visual categories from noisy internet image–text pairs and performed zero-shot classification from natural-language labels; DALL·E treated pixels as a generative token sequence.
events.meaning: Natural language became a general interface to perception and generation, establishing the technical line that later powered text-to-image products and multimodal assistants.
events.reaction: The compositional images were startling, but researchers immediately noted CLIP’s counting, fine-grained recognition, bias, and dataset-opacity problems.
events.gained: OpenAI and labs with web-scale paired data.
events.lost: task-specific vision pipelines and smaller teams dependent on labeled datasets.

events.title: NVIDIA announces the Grace data-center CPU
events.development: NVIDIA moved beyond selling accelerators by announcing an Arm-based CPU designed to sit beside GPUs in giant AI and high-performance-computing systems.
events.technicalChange: Grace emphasized high-bandwidth coherent CPU–GPU communication and memory capacity rather than treating the GPU as a PCIe peripheral.
events.meaning: NVIDIA’s ambition expanded from valuable chip supplier to full-system architect—CPU, GPU, interconnect, networking, libraries, and reference systems.
events.reaction: Investors read the move as a direct challenge to Intel and AMD; customers saw a possible remedy for the data-feeding bottleneck around accelerators.
events.lost: incumbent x86 control over the AI server’s host processor.

events.title: Cerebras unveils WSE-2 and CS-2
events.development: Cerebras introduced its second wafer-scale processor and system.
events.technicalChange: WSE-2 placed 2.6 trillion transistors and 850,000 AI-optimized cores across a whole 7-nanometer wafer, avoiding the package-to-package links required by GPU clusters.
events.meaning: The company made a credible architectural bet that keeping compute and memory movement on one enormous die could simplify training and later make inference unusually fast.
events.reaction: The engineering was widely admired; commercial skepticism centered on yield, software portability, and whether a wafer-scale system could overcome CUDA’s ecosystem.
events.gained: Cerebras as a technically serious alternative.
events.lost: no immediate NVIDIA share, but the assumption that all frontier compute had to be conventional packaged GPUs weakened.

events.title: The European Commission proposes the AI Act
events.development: The Commission proposed the first horizontal, economy-wide AI law, built around prohibited, high-risk, transparency, and minimal-risk categories.
events.technicalChange: It shifted oversight from sector-by-sector ethics to ex ante conformity duties based on use risk; the initial proposal predated ChatGPT and did not yet have the final general-purpose-model regime.
events.meaning: Brussels positioned access to the EU market as leverage to set global compliance norms.
events.reaction: Rights groups welcomed enforceability but sought stronger protections; startups and industry warned that broad definitions and conformity costs could suppress European innovation.
events.lost: deployers assuming AI could remain governed only by product terms.

events.title: Google presents LaMDA
events.development: Google showed a Transformer trained specifically for open-ended dialogue.
events.technicalChange: LaMDA was optimized for conversation across arbitrary topics and evaluated on sensibleness, specificity, interestingness, factuality, and safety rather than next-token loss alone.
events.meaning: Google had core chatbot technology before the ChatGPT era, but treated it as a research and safety problem rather than an immediately distributable product.
events.reaction: The fluent demonstrations drew enthusiasm and caution; Google’s measured rollout was initially seen as responsibility, but later as evidence of product hesitation.
events.lost: none immediately; in hindsight, Google’s distribution advantage remained unused.

events.title: Anthropic emerges as an alignment-first frontier lab
events.development: Former OpenAI researchers announced a $124 million financing for Anthropic, founded at the beginning of the year.
events.technicalChange: The new lab’s program centered on steerability, robustness, interpretability, and empirical scaling research rather than a consumer product.
events.meaning: Frontier-model talent and safety research were no longer concentrated inside OpenAI, and a second independent U.S. lab could attract the capital required for large training runs.
events.reaction: The founding was read both as a principled safety effort and as the first important OpenAI diaspora.
events.gained: Anthropic and investors willing to fund pre-product research.
events.lost: OpenAI’s monopoly on its founding cohort and alignment narrative.

events.title: GitHub Copilot enters technical preview
events.development: GitHub and OpenAI launched an in-editor “AI pair programmer,” initially powered by Codex.
events.technicalChange: Instead of a chat box, the model continuously conditioned on the open file and nearby repository context to synthesize code and tests inside the IDE.
events.meaning: Code generation acquired a high-frequency distribution surface and a feedback loop across millions of developers. It also foreshadowed the importance of a harness: the same base model was more valuable when embedded in workflow.
events.reaction: Developers alternated between delight at useful completions and anger over licensing, security, attribution, and memorized code.
events.lost: standalone coding assistants and model vendors without developer distribution.

events.title: AI21 opens Jurassic-1 Studio
events.development: AI21 Labs released API access to Jurassic-1, including a 178-billion-parameter “Jumbo” model.
events.technicalChange: The family competed with GPT-3 on general text generation while exposing a developer studio outside a U.S. hyperscaler.
events.meaning: The commercial foundation-model market began to look like a platform category rather than an OpenAI-only API.
events.reaction: The launch strengthened Israel’s position in applied NLP, though limited consumer distribution kept it below GPT-3 in public awareness.
events.gained: AI21 and enterprise buyers seeking supplier choice.
events.lost: a small amount of OpenAI API exclusivity.

events.title: OpenAI releases Codex through its API
events.development: OpenAI made its GPT-3 descendant for programming available in private beta.
events.technicalChange: Codex was further trained on source code and could translate natural-language instructions into executable programs across languages; GitHub Copilot was its first major deployment.
events.meaning: Software became both model output and a tool for extending model capability—an idea that later defined coding agents and general computer-using agents.
events.reaction: Live demos looked magical, while evaluations and users exposed brittle intent-following, insecure code, and dependence on tests.
events.gained: OpenAI, GitHub, and developers who could supervise generated code.
events.lost: purely autocomplete-based tools.

events.title: DeepMind publishes Gopher and a risk taxonomy
events.development: DeepMind introduced a 280-billion-parameter language model alongside work on retrieval and ethical/social risks.
events.technicalChange: Gopher substantially improved reading comprehension, fact checking, and MMLU, yet scale did little for some logic and common-sense tasks; the companion analysis catalogued predictable failure modes.
events.meaning: Raw parameter scaling still worked, but the release documented a ceiling: larger models could become more confidently wrong.
events.reaction: Researchers respected the unusually detailed risk analysis but noted that the weights and product access remained closed.
events.lost: the simplistic claim that parameters alone produced general reasoning.

sources.label: Google DeepMind: Gopher, retrieval, and risks

events.title: NIST begins turning AI risk into an operational framework
events.development: After a July request for information, NIST issued the concept paper that became the U.S. AI Risk Management Framework.
events.technicalChange: The initiative framed AI risk as a continuous organizational process spanning governance, mapping, measurement, and management—not a one-time model accuracy test.
events.meaning: The U.S. began building a voluntary, standards-led alternative to Europe’s binding risk regulation.
events.reaction: Industry favored flexibility; civil-rights advocates questioned whether voluntary guidance could constrain high-impact uses.
events.gained: NIST, standards teams, and large firms able to operationalize governance.
events.lost: no actor directly, though undocumented “move fast” deployments faced rising scrutiny.

events.title: InstructGPT makes RLHF the deployment recipe
events.development: OpenAI deployed InstructGPT as the default family in its API.
events.technicalChange: Human demonstrations trained a supervised model; human preference rankings trained a reward model; reinforcement learning then optimized the model against that signal. A 1.3B InstructGPT was preferred to 175B GPT-3 despite being over 100 times smaller.
events.meaning: Post-training, instruction following, and perceived helpfulness became at least as strategically important as pretraining scale. This recipe directly preceded ChatGPT.
events.reaction: The results were celebrated as practical alignment, with caveats about annotator values, sycophancy, and reward hacking.
events.gained: OpenAI and firms controlling feedback pipelines.
events.lost: labs focused only on larger pretrained checkpoints.

sources.label: OpenAI: Aligning language models to follow instructions

events.title: NVIDIA announces Hopper H100
events.development: NVIDIA introduced the 80-billion-transistor H100 and Hopper architecture, with production availability later in 2022.
events.technicalChange: The Transformer Engine dynamically used FP8 and FP16, fourth-generation NVLink improved scale-up communication, and systems paired H100 with NVSwitch, Quantum-2 InfiniBand, Grace, and ConnectX networking.
events.meaning: H100 became the scarce physical substrate of the generative-AI boom and made low-precision Transformer acceleration a first-class architectural feature.
events.reaction: Initial attention was technical; after ChatGPT, allocations became a strategic asset and a proxy for lab credibility.
events.gained: NVIDIA, TSMC, HBM suppliers, and clouds with allocations.
events.lost: accelerator rivals and labs unable to secure clusters.

events.title: Google publishes the 540B-parameter PaLM
events.development: Google trained Pathways Language Model across 6,144 TPU v4 chips.
events.technicalChange: A dense 540B Transformer used Pathways infrastructure and demonstrated strong few-shot learning, multilingual transfer, code ability, and step-by-step prompting; Google highlighted discontinuous “emergent” capabilities at scale.
events.meaning: Google remained at the model frontier and showed that its vertically integrated TPU stack could train at immense scale.
events.reaction: PaLM’s benchmark results impressed researchers, while its lack of broad access limited developer momentum.
events.lost: outside developers, who still could not build on the strongest Google model.

events.title: DALL·E 2 combines CLIP semantics with diffusion
events.development: OpenAI previewed a much higher-resolution text-to-image system with editing and variation.
events.technicalChange: A prior mapped captions into CLIP image embeddings, and a diffusion decoder produced images, improving photorealism and compositional control over the first DALL·E.
events.meaning: Generative AI’s economic and copyright implications became visible first in creative work, months before ChatGPT did the same for text.
events.reaction: Wonder at image quality mixed with alarm from artists over consent, dataset provenance, stylistic imitation, deepfakes, and job displacement.
events.lost: stock-image intermediaries and some confidence in the durability of human-only creative production.

events.title: Chinchilla overturns the “bigger is better” allocation rule
events.development: DeepMind reported that a 70B model trained on 1.3 trillion tokens beat 280B Gopher at the same training compute.
events.technicalChange: Its scaling-law analysis showed many large models were undertrained: compute should grow model size and training tokens roughly together.
events.meaning: The field redirected budgets toward much more data per parameter, producing smaller models that were also cheaper to serve. LLaMA, DeepSeek, and many later families followed the compute-optimal logic.
events.reaction: The paper was rapidly absorbed as a new default recipe.
events.gained: data curation, efficient training, and inference economics.
events.lost: parameter count as the primary prestige metric.

events.title: Flamingo demonstrates few-shot visual-language learning
events.development: DeepMind introduced an 80B visual-language model that accepted interleaved images and text.
events.technicalChange: A frozen vision encoder and language model were joined by Perceiver resampling and gated cross-attention, allowing one model to adapt to many image/video tasks from a handful of examples.
events.meaning: Multimodality no longer meant only caption generation; it could be an in-context interface to perception.
events.reaction: The research was influential, but the closed checkpoint again limited Google/DeepMind’s ecosystem capture.
events.lost: specialized vision-language pipelines; Google gained science prestige but little developer lock-in.

events.title: Meta releases OPT-175B for controlled research access
events.development: Meta shared pretrained models, training code, logs, and smaller baselines, with the 175B weights available to approved researchers under a noncommercial license.
events.technicalChange: OPT reproduced GPT-3-class scale with unusually extensive operational disclosure and more efficient distributed training.
events.meaning: Reproducibility and access became an explicit counter-strategy to closed APIs.
events.reaction: Researchers welcomed the logs and weights but criticized restricted access and a license that was not open source.
events.gained: Meta’s open-science identity and academic researchers.
events.lost: closed labs’ information advantage, though only modestly because access was gated.

events.title: GitHub Copilot becomes generally available
events.development: GitHub converted its Codex-based coding assistant from preview into a paid product.
events.technicalChange: Production telemetry, IDE integration, and low-latency completion turned an imperfect model into a dependable habit, while filters attempted to reduce verbatim public-code suggestions.
events.meaning: Copilot became the first scaled, recurring-revenue application of a code LLM and proved workflow placement could matter more than owning the base model.
events.reaction: Adoption was rapid, but the open-source community’s licensing objections hardened into litigation later in the year.
events.lost: competing IDE assistants and maintainers without bargaining power over training use.

events.title: BigScience releases BLOOM
events.development: More than 1,000 researchers released a 176B multilingual model trained transparently on France’s Jean Zay supercomputer.
events.technicalChange: BLOOM covered 46 natural and 13 programming languages and published data, training, and governance details under a responsible-use license.
events.meaning: A distributed public collaboration proved that a non-hyperscaler coalition could train a giant model and established Hugging Face as the neutral exchange layer for open models.
events.reaction: The process was hailed as a landmark for transparency and language inclusion, though quality and inference cost limited mass use.
events.gained: Hugging Face, public compute, and multilingual research.
events.lost: the claim that only private labs could organize frontier-scale training.

events.title: The U.S. CHIPS and Science Act becomes law
events.development: The United States funded domestic semiconductor manufacturing incentives and research, including $39 billion for manufacturing and $11 billion for semiconductor R&D.
events.technicalChange: This was not a model change but an upstream capacity intervention: grants, tax incentives, workforce programs, and advanced-computing research aimed to reduce dependence on East Asian fabrication.
events.meaning: AI compute became industrial and national-security policy, not merely cloud procurement.
events.reaction: The law drew bipartisan support; critics warned that fabs take years, subsidies can become corporate welfare, and advanced packaging remained a gap.
events.gained: Intel, TSMC’s U.S. plans, Samsung, U.S. equipment and construction ecosystems.
events.lost: some strategic comfort in geographically concentrated supply chains.

sources.label: Congressional Research Service on semiconductors and AI

events.title: OpenAI open-sources Whisper
events.development: OpenAI released model weights and inference code for multilingual speech recognition and translation.
events.technicalChange: A straightforward encoder–decoder Transformer trained on 680,000 hours of diverse supervised audio performed language identification, timestamping, transcription, and translation in one model and generalized robustly across datasets.
events.meaning: High-quality speech interfaces became a commodity component for developers and later supplied the “ears” of multimodal agents.
events.reaction: Developers adopted it quickly because local deployment was useful even when benchmark-specialized systems scored better.
events.gained: OpenAI goodwill and the open developer ecosystem.
events.lost: proprietary transcription APIs’ differentiation.

events.title: LangChain popularizes application-side orchestration
events.development: LangChain emerged as an open-source framework for chaining prompts, models, retrieval, memory, and tools.
events.technicalChange: It standardized interchangeable components around LLM calls and rapidly accumulated integrations.
events.meaning: Developers could prototype retrieval-augmented and agent-like applications without waiting for model vendors to ship a full platform.
events.reaction: Adoption was explosive; experienced engineers also criticized abstraction churn, hidden prompts, and production complexity.
events.lost: some model-platform lock-in and the simplicity of direct API calls.

events.title: GLM-130B provides a bilingual open foundation model
events.development: The Tsinghua/Zhipu team released GLM-130B, a Chinese–English 130B model and training code.
events.technicalChange: The General Language Model objective combined autoregressive generation with blank infilling, and the project emphasized reproducible training of a very large bilingual checkpoint.
events.meaning: China’s open-model ecosystem acquired a large domestic base before ChatGLM and the later commercial GLM family.
events.reaction: Researchers welcomed rare access at this scale; practical use was constrained by substantial inference hardware.
events.lost: Western-only assumptions about open frontier-scale capability.

events.title: ReAct formalizes the reasoning–action loop
events.development: Researchers introduced prompting that interleaved natural-language reasoning traces with actions in an external environment.
events.technicalChange: Instead of answering in one pass, a model could plan, call a search or environment tool, observe the result, and revise.
events.meaning: ReAct became the conceptual skeleton of many later agent harnesses: model, tool schema, observation, loop, stop condition.
events.reaction: Results on question answering and interactive tasks were compelling, but loops remained fragile and expensive.
events.lost: the idea that model weights alone determined application capability.

events.title: U.S. export controls target China’s AI-compute stack
events.development: The Commerce Department restricted advanced computing chips, supercomputer end uses, semiconductor-manufacturing equipment, and U.S.-person support for advanced Chinese fabs.
events.technicalChange: Controls reached beyond exports from America through foreign-direct-product rules and process thresholds for logic, DRAM, and NAND.
events.meaning: Access to frontier accelerators and the tools to manufacture them became a central instrument of geopolitical containment.
events.reaction: U.S. security analysts called the package unprecedented; industry warned about lost sales and accelerated Chinese substitution.
events.gained: U.S. export-control authority and allied equipment leverage.
events.lost: NVIDIA’s unrestricted China market, Chinese labs’ access to top parts, and TSMC’s freedom to fabricate for some clients.

sources.label: U.S. Bureau of Industry and Security

events.title: Meta releases, then withdraws Galactica’s demo
events.development: Meta launched a 120B scientific-language model demo and removed it after three days.
events.technicalChange: Galactica was trained on papers, textbooks, reference material, and scientific knowledge formats, but generated plausible false citations and confident nonsense.
events.meaning: Domain pretraining did not solve hallucination; fluent scientific form could amplify epistemic risk.
events.reaction: Critics rapidly documented fabrications and harmful outputs, while some researchers argued that the takedown punished open experimentation.
events.gained: demands for model cards, evaluation, and staged release.
events.lost: Meta’s confidence in direct public demos and the premise that specialist corpora guaranteed reliability.

events.title: ChatGPT turns an alignment technique into a mass-market interface
events.development: OpenAI launched a free research preview based on a GPT-3.5-series conversational model.
events.technicalChange: Dialogue-format RLHF let the system follow instructions, preserve conversational context, admit mistakes, challenge premises, and refuse some unsafe requests. The underlying advances were evolutionary; the frictionless product and feedback loop were revolutionary.
events.meaning: Tens of millions of people could directly experience a general-purpose language model, setting off emergency product launches, education bans, investment waves, and policy work.
events.reaction: Awe, playful experimentation, and productivity enthusiasm coexisted with alarm over cheating, hallucinations, bias, copyright, and labor displacement.
events.gained: OpenAI and Microsoft; “chat” became the default interface to AI.
events.lost: Google’s consumer-AI narrative, incumbent search assumptions, and every lab without mass distribution.
events.whyItFeltDifferent: This was the first mass experiential break in the timeline. People did not need an API, a paper, or a carefully staged demo: they could ask follow-up questions in ordinary language and watch a machine draft, explain, transform, and improvise. The public conversation shifted almost overnight from whether language models were useful to what their widespread use would disrupt.

events.title: Microsoft deepens its OpenAI alliance
events.development: Microsoft announced the third phase of its partnership, a multiyear, multibillion-dollar investment widely reported as roughly $10 billion.
events.technicalChange: The agreement paired frontier-model research with dedicated Azure supercomputing, exclusive cloud provision, product distribution, and shared commercialization rights.
events.meaning: OpenAI obtained the capital and compute to stay at the frontier; Microsoft bought the fastest route to put generative AI into search, productivity software, GitHub, and Azure.
events.reaction: Markets saw a potentially decisive coup, while customers and regulators worried about dependence on one model–cloud bloc.
events.lost: Google’s cloud/search narrative, AWS’s access to the hottest lab, and independent model hosts.

events.title: NIST publishes AI RMF 1.0
events.development: NIST released a voluntary framework for organizations designing, deploying, or using AI.
events.technicalChange: The core organized risk practice into Govern, Map, Measure, Manage, covering validity, safety, security, accountability, transparency, explainability, privacy, and harmful bias across the lifecycle.
events.meaning: The United States now had a common operational vocabulary that procurement teams and future executive orders could reference without immediately legislating model design.
events.reaction: Companies welcomed a flexible standard; critics noted that voluntary adoption and self-measurement left enforcement gaps.
events.lost: ad hoc internal ethics principles with no measurable process.

events.title: Google announces Bard and Microsoft launches the new Bing
events.development: Google rushed a LaMDA-powered Bard preview announcement on February 6; Microsoft publicly integrated an OpenAI “Prometheus” model into Bing and Edge on February 7.
events.technicalChange: Both systems grounded chat in live search results and generated synthesized answers, citations, and follow-ups.
events.meaning: The web’s dominant discovery and advertising interface was suddenly contestable.
events.reaction: Bing’s surreal, emotionally manipulative long chats generated fascination and concern; an error in Google’s Bard demonstration helped erase about $100 billion from Alphabet’s market value, crystallizing the perception that Google was on defense.
events.lost: Google’s aura of unassailable AI execution and traditional link lists.

events.title: Meta releases LLaMA to researchers
events.development: Meta introduced 7B, 13B, 33B, and 65B foundation models under a research license; the weights leaked within days.
events.technicalChange: Trained on public data with far more tokens per parameter than earlier giants, LLaMA-13B competed with GPT-3 while fitting on far less hardware.
events.meaning: Chinchilla-style efficient training gave academics and hobbyists a strong base for local fine-tuning; the leak made access controls largely irreversible.
events.reaction: Developers treated it as the birth of the modern local-LLM ecosystem, while safety and copyright concerns accompanied uncontrolled redistribution.
events.lost: closed API vendors’ scarcity advantage.

events.title: GPT-4, Claude, and ChatGLM-6B arrive on the same day
events.development: OpenAI released GPT-4; Anthropic publicly introduced Claude; Tsinghua/Zhipu released the bilingual ChatGLM-6B.
events.technicalChange: GPT-4 accepted images as well as text and sharply improved reasoning, coding, safety, and reliability; Claude foregrounded Constitutional AI and long, steerable conversation; ChatGLM used quantization to run locally on consumer-grade hardware.
events.meaning: The market split into three durable strategies: premium closed frontier models, a safety/enterprise challenger, and efficient domestic/open-weight ecosystems.
events.reaction: GPT-4’s exam and coding results were received as a major leap, but OpenAI’s refusal to disclose architecture, data, or compute drew criticism. Claude was quieter but well reviewed; ChatGLM accelerated China’s answer to ChatGPT.
events.lost: GPT-3.5-class startups and Western-only views of the race.

events.title: Microsoft announces 365 Copilot
events.development: Microsoft embedded generative AI into Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook, and Teams.
events.technicalChange: The “Copilot system” combined an LLM with Microsoft Graph organizational data and application-specific commands rather than exposing a generic chat model.
events.meaning: Enterprise context, permissions, and workflow integration became a defensible layer above commodity model calls.
events.reaction: Demos generated enormous productivity expectations, followed by caution about pricing, security, hallucinated business facts, and measurable return on investment.
events.lost: standalone enterprise assistants lacking access to system-of-record data.

events.title: ChatGPT plugins connect models to the outside world
events.development: OpenAI introduced plugins for web browsing, code execution, retrieval, and third-party actions.
events.technicalChange: A model could select an API from a machine-readable manifest, construct calls, and incorporate observations into a response.
events.meaning: ChatGPT began changing from an isolated text generator into an action platform; prompt injection and untrusted tool output became security problems.
events.reaction: Developers anticipated an “app store for AI,” but the ecosystem remained fragmented and was later superseded by custom GPTs, function calling, and MCP.
events.gained: OpenAI as gatekeeper and API-owning services.
events.lost: unaffiliated chat wrappers; browser safety boundaries weakened.

events.title: Auto-GPT and BabyAGI ignite the autonomous-agent wave
events.development: Open-source projects wrapped GPT-4 in recursive planning, memory, browsing, and tool-execution loops.
events.technicalChange: A high-level goal was decomposed into tasks; the model acted, inspected results, stored context, and created the next task without a human prompt at every step.
events.meaning: The agent concept became legible to millions of developers, even though reliability was poor.
events.reaction: Viral demos promised autonomous companies; real use exposed infinite loops, compounding errors, token cost, and dangerous permissions.
events.gained: open-source harness builders and tool APIs.
events.lost: confidence that a clever prompt loop alone constituted dependable autonomy.

events.title: Italy temporarily blocks ChatGPT
events.development: Italy’s data-protection authority ordered a temporary limitation after a data breach and raised questions about lawful training data, notice, accuracy, and age verification; access returned after OpenAI made changes.
events.technicalChange: The intervention forced product controls—privacy disclosures, an objection mechanism, age gates, and options concerning chat history—not a model redesign.
events.meaning: GDPR could constrain a frontier service before the AI Act existed, and national regulators could act independently.
events.reaction: Privacy advocates welcomed enforcement; many users and politicians called a national block disproportionate.
events.gained: European data-protection authorities and users’ procedural rights.
events.lost: OpenAI’s assumption of uniform global rollout.

events.title: PaLM 2 powers Google’s product counterattack
events.development: Google released PaLM 2 in Gecko, Otter, Bison, and Unicorn sizes and put it across Bard, Workspace, security, and cloud products.
events.technicalChange: A more multilingual, code-heavy, and reasoning-oriented mixture of pretraining objectives improved efficiency relative to the much larger PaLM. Specialized Med-PaLM 2 and Sec-PaLM variants targeted regulated domains.
events.meaning: Google translated research into broad product deployment and emphasized a full family rather than one monolith.
events.reaction: The release reduced panic about Google’s technical position, although Bard still trailed ChatGPT in mindshare.
events.lost: some Microsoft narrative momentum.

events.title: Claude moves to a 100K-token context window
events.development: Anthropic expanded Claude’s context to roughly 75,000 words.
events.technicalChange: Users could place whole reports, books, or codebases into one prompt instead of relying on chunked retrieval, with a “needle” fact recalled from long documents.
events.meaning: Context length became a headline competitive dimension and a substitute—sometimes an expensive one—for retrieval infrastructure.
events.reaction: Enterprise users valued document analysis; researchers cautioned that maximum input length did not imply uniform attention or reasoning across it.
events.lost: OpenAI’s context lead and some early RAG middleware differentiation.

events.title: OpenAI standardizes function calling
events.development: GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 Turbo gained structured function calling; GPT-3.5 also gained a 16K variant.
events.technicalChange: Developers described functions with JSON Schema, and the model emitted machine-readable arguments rather than prose that applications had to parse.
events.meaning: Reliable tool routing moved into the model API and became the core primitive for production agents.
events.reaction: Developers embraced the reduction in brittle prompt parsing, while security engineers warned that valid JSON did not make an action truthful or authorized.
events.gained: OpenAI’s developer platform and typed API ecosystems.
events.lost: bespoke parsers and some third-party orchestration glue.

events.title: ChatGLM2-6B improves local Chinese deployment
events.development: The ChatGLM team released its second 6B bilingual chat model.
events.technicalChange: It used a more efficient GLM architecture, 1.4 trillion training tokens, multi-query attention, 32K context, and substantially faster inference while retaining low-bit local deployment.
events.meaning: Chinese developers obtained an increasingly capable base model independent of U.S. APIs and accessible without a data-center cluster.
events.reaction: The family spread through domestic research and applications, even as top closed models remained stronger.
events.lost: imported API dependence.

events.title: Code Interpreter turns chat into a sandboxed analytical computer
events.development: OpenAI rolled Code Interpreter out to ChatGPT Plus and made the GPT-4 API generally available.
events.technicalChange: The model could write and execute Python in an isolated environment, iterate after errors, inspect uploaded files, calculate, chart, and return artifacts.
events.meaning: Execution let a model verify work and perform transformations it could not reliably simulate in tokens—a direct ancestor of today’s general agent computer environments.
events.reaction: Users called it a junior data analyst; limitations included session state, opaque packages, privacy concerns, and the model’s ability to misread successful-looking output.
events.lost: simple data-analysis wrappers and the “chat is only text” framing.

events.title: Claude 2 becomes a public ChatGPT-class competitor
events.development: Anthropic released Claude 2 in the U.S. and U.K. with web chat and API access.
events.technicalChange: The model improved coding, math, reasoning, safety, and 100K-context document work over Claude 1.3 while allowing much longer outputs.
events.meaning: Anthropic moved from partner-integrated model supplier to a direct consumer and developer brand.
events.reaction: Reviewers praised its writing and long-document behavior but found it more conservative and sometimes less capable than GPT-4.
events.gained: Anthropic and customers seeking a second frontier provider.
events.lost: OpenAI’s uncontested premium-chat position.

events.title: Llama 2 makes open weights commercially deployable
events.development: Meta released 7B, 13B, and 70B base and chat models with a custom commercial license and Microsoft as preferred cloud partner.
events.technicalChange: Models were trained on two trillion tokens; chat variants used supervised fine-tuning and RLHF, and context doubled to 4K.
events.meaning: Companies could fine-tune and self-host a strong modern LLM rather than pay per token, giving open weights a sustainable commercial center.
events.reaction: Developers celebrated access; critics objected that usage restrictions and a 700-million-user clause made “open source” inaccurate.
events.gained: Meta, Azure, Hugging Face, cloud/GPU hosts, fine-tuning startups.
events.lost: closed API price power.

events.title: Alibaba opens Qwen-7B and Qwen-7B-Chat
events.development: Alibaba Cloud released the first public Qwen checkpoints, followed by Qwen-VL, Qwen-Audio, larger Qwen-14B/72B, and improved chat variants through the rest of 2023.
events.technicalChange: The family combined Chinese–English language competence with code, tool use, vision-language grounding, and later audio under progressively more permissive licenses.
events.meaning: Alibaba turned one model into an extensible multimodal open ecosystem and a distribution asset for ModelScope and its cloud.
events.reaction: Early attention was regional; rapid quality gains made Qwen one of the default bases for Chinese and global fine-tuning.
events.lost: Meta’s near-monopoly on useful open weights.

events.title: China’s generative-AI rules take effect
events.development: Interim Measures required public generative-AI providers to protect personal information, respect intellectual property, label some generated content, address illegal outputs, and comply with security/filing requirements.
events.technicalChange: Compared with the harsher draft, final rules focused on services offered to the public and explicitly paired control with state support for innovation.
events.meaning: China created the first binding national regime aimed specifically at generative AI, coupling content governance with industrial policy.
events.reaction: Firms welcomed more workable scope but still faced censorship, registration, and data obligations foreign rivals could not easily satisfy.
events.lost: unregistered services and foreign platforms.

events.title: Mistral 7B gives Europe a high-quality open model company
events.development: Four-month-old Mistral AI released a 7.3B Apache-2.0 model.
events.technicalChange: Grouped-query attention reduced inference memory and sliding-window attention handled sequences efficiently; the small model beat Llama 2 13B on many benchmarks.
events.meaning: Strong architecture and data could outrun parameter scale, and a European startup could compete globally without first shipping a giant model.
events.reaction: The release was embraced by local-LLM developers and validated Mistral’s large seed valuation.
events.lost: Meta’s mindshare among compact-model users.

events.title: Moonshot AI launches Kimi Chat with 128K context
events.development: Beijing startup Moonshot AI launched Kimi, initially distinguished by processing roughly 200,000 Chinese characters in a conversation.
events.technicalChange: Long-context attention and document ingestion targeted research, legal, financial, and office workflows rather than only casual chat.
events.meaning: A new Chinese lab acquired a clear product wedge—long documents—and a consumer feedback loop independent of the better-funded internet giants.
events.reaction: Demand surged as users tested entire reports and books, establishing Kimi as a national challenger.
events.lost: Baidu, Alibaba, and Zhipu mindshare at the consumer edge.

events.title: The U.S. closes chip-control workarounds
events.development: BIS updated the 2022 rules to capture NVIDIA’s China-specific A800/H800-class products, more manufacturing equipment, additional destinations, and evasion routes.
events.technicalChange: A performance-density threshold replaced reliance on interconnect bandwidth and aimed to cover future workaround designs.
events.meaning: Export control became an iterative technical contest, with each accelerator SKU and training topology potentially altering legal access.
events.reaction: China condemned containment; NVIDIA warned that abrupt restrictions could harm its competitive position while preparing lower-spec parts.
events.gained: BIS’s reach and domestic Chinese accelerator incentives.
events.lost: NVIDIA China revenue flexibility and Chinese frontier labs’ supply certainty.

events.title: U.S. executive order and G7 code put frontier models under formal oversight
events.development: President Biden signed Executive Order 14110 as the G7 published its Hiroshima Process code for advanced AI developers.
events.technicalChange: The U.S. order used the Defense Production Act to require certain developers to report large training runs and safety-test results, tasked NIST with standards, and addressed biosecurity, cybersecurity, civil rights, procurement, labor, and content authentication.
events.meaning: Voluntary commitments began hardening into federal reporting and evaluation infrastructure.
events.reaction: Safety advocates welcomed breadth but questioned thresholds and enforcement; industry preferred the executive approach to premature legislation.
events.gained: the White House, NIST, Commerce, and model-evaluation institutions.
events.lost: secrecy around the largest training runs.

sources.label: White House budgetary/legal record for EO 14110

events.title: The Bletchley Declaration creates a frontier-safety diplomatic track
events.development: Twenty-eight governments and the EU—including China and the United States—agreed that frontier AI could pose severe, even catastrophic, risks and warranted shared research, evaluation, and governance.
events.technicalChange: The summit established government access to pre-deployment model testing as an international objective and launched recurring scientific reporting.
events.meaning: Frontier safety briefly became a domain of great-power cooperation despite the chip war.
events.reaction: Inclusion of China was treated as a diplomatic success; critics noted that the declaration was nonbinding and vague.
events.gained: the U.K. AI Safety Institute and external evaluators.
events.lost: labs’ claim that self-evaluation alone was sufficient.

events.title: OpenAI DevDay launches GPT-4 Turbo, custom GPTs, and Assistants API
events.development: OpenAI bundled a 128K GPT-4 Turbo, lower prices, JSON mode, parallel function calls, reproducible outputs, updated knowledge, DALL·E 3, TTS, Whisper v3, GPTs, and the Assistants API.
events.technicalChange: Hosted threads, retrieval, Code Interpreter, tools, and instruction packages moved stateful agent infrastructure onto OpenAI’s platform.
events.meaning: OpenAI tried to own both the frontier model and the application runtime, while natural-language-configured GPTs lowered the barrier to building assistants.
events.reaction: Developers were enthusiastic about price and context but feared their startups had been absorbed as features.
events.lost: “wrapper” startups, some orchestration vendors, and rival APIs without hosted tools.

events.title: NVIDIA introduces H200
events.development: NVIDIA refreshed Hopper with HBM3e memory.
events.technicalChange: H200 increased accelerator memory to 141 GB and bandwidth to 4.8 TB/s, allowing larger models and KV caches to fit with less communication.
events.meaning: Memory capacity and bandwidth—not only tensor FLOPS—became decisive for long-context and high-throughput inference.
events.reaction: Cloud and server partners committed quickly; the product also showed NVIDIA could extend a winning architecture before Blackwell.
events.gained: NVIDIA, HBM supplier SK hynix, and clouds securing early inventory.
events.lost: rivals whose nominal compute lacked comparable memory systems.

events.title: Microsoft unveils Maia 100 and Cobalt 100
events.development: Microsoft announced its first in-house AI accelerator and Arm server CPU.
events.technicalChange: Maia 100 was co-designed with OpenAI for Azure AI workloads, paired with a custom liquid-cooled server and network architecture; Cobalt targeted general cloud efficiency.
events.meaning: Even NVIDIA’s largest customers intended to own silicon and system design to control cost, capacity, and workload optimization.
events.reaction: The move was seen as long-term NVIDIA leverage rather than an immediate CUDA replacement.
events.gained: Microsoft’s vertical integration and Marvell/TSMC-style custom silicon ecosystems.
events.lost: some future NVIDIA pricing power and x86 exclusivity.

events.title: OpenAI’s board fires and reinstates Sam Altman
events.development: The nonprofit board removed Altman for not being “consistently candid”; employee revolt, investor pressure, and Microsoft’s offer to hire the team led to his return and a largely replaced board.
events.technicalChange: None to the models; the change was governance under frontier-scale capital pressure.
events.meaning: The episode showed that formal nonprofit control could be overwhelmed by employee mobility, compute dependency, and a strategic investor. Microsoft obtained a nonvoting board-observer path, and commercialization advocates emerged stronger.
events.reaction: The week was treated as both corporate farce and a constitutional crisis for AI governance.
events.lost: the former board, effective-altruist influence, and confidence in the capped-profit structure’s checks.

events.title: Claude 2.1 doubles context to 200K
events.development: Anthropic released Claude 2.1 with a 200K window, lower hallucination rates, system prompts, and beta tool use.
events.technicalChange: The update targeted enterprise reliability: Anthropic reported fewer false statements and fewer claims that absent material appeared in a supplied document.
events.meaning: Long context matured from spectacle into document-grounded enterprise infrastructure, and Claude gained the primitives for tools before its public computer-use push.
events.reaction: The enormous window drew praise, while “lost in the middle” tests across the field tempered claims about usable context.
events.lost: smaller-context rivals and naïve retrieval-only stacks.

events.title: Google releases Gemini 1.0 in Ultra, Pro, and Nano tiers
events.development: Google DeepMind introduced Gemini, with Pro powering Bard, Nano running on devices, and Ultra reserved for later release.
events.technicalChange: Gemini was trained from the outset across text, images, audio, video, and code rather than attaching separate perception modules; TPU v4 and v5e trained the family.
events.meaning: Google unified Brain and DeepMind’s model effort and used its full stack—research, TPUs, Android, Search, Workspace, and Cloud—to reenter the frontier race.
events.reaction: Benchmark claims suggested Ultra could beat GPT-4, but a highly edited demo and delayed access produced skepticism.
events.lost: Bard/PaLM branding and some trust in launch marketing.

events.title: AMD ships MI300X and ROCm 6
events.development: AMD made its Instinct MI300X accelerator and MI300A CPU–GPU APU available with commitments from Microsoft, Meta, Oracle, and major server vendors.
events.technicalChange: MI300X used chiplets, 192 GB of HBM3, 5.3 TB/s bandwidth, FP8, and an eight-accelerator 1.5 TB platform; ROCm 6 improved the software path for PyTorch, vLLM, and FlashAttention.
events.meaning: AMD finally fielded a credible memory-rich alternative for large-model inference and some training.
events.reaction: Customers welcomed supply and price competition, but CUDA maturity remained the central objection.
events.lost: a measure of NVIDIA’s hardware monopoly, not its software moat.

events.title: EU negotiators reach a political deal on the AI Act
events.development: Parliament and Council negotiators agreed on the law’s final architecture, adding general-purpose AI and systemic-risk model obligations after ChatGPT changed the legislative facts.
events.technicalChange: Providers of powerful general-purpose models would face documentation, copyright-policy, evaluation, incident-reporting, cybersecurity, and systemic-risk duties; prohibited and high-risk uses retained stricter controls.
events.meaning: The “Brussels effect” moved upstream from applications into foundation-model governance.
events.reaction: European leaders called it historic; rights groups warned about law-enforcement exceptions, and model developers objected to uncertain thresholds and cost.
events.lost: opaque model development and smaller EU firms facing fixed compliance costs.

events.title: Mixtral 8×7B validates sparse mixture-of-experts for open models
events.development: Mistral released an Apache-2.0 sparse mixture-of-experts model via a magnet link before publishing details.
events.technicalChange: Each token routed through two of eight feed-forward experts, giving about 46.7B total parameters but roughly 12.9B active per token, with 32K context.
events.meaning: MoE offered high quality without paying dense-model compute on every token and became central to later Qwen, DeepSeek, Kimi, and GLM designs.
events.reaction: The unconventional release delighted open-source developers; its memory footprint reminded users that low active compute did not mean small weights.
events.lost: dense scaling as the only accepted route.

events.title: Zhipu launches the GLM-4 generation
events.development: Zhipu introduced GLM-4, later extending the family with GLM-4-Air, 9B open weights, vision, and “All Tools” agent variants.
events.technicalChange: The generation substantially improved Chinese/English reasoning, coding, long context, multimodal understanding, and autonomous use of web browsing, Python, and APIs.
events.meaning: Zhipu progressed from the academic ChatGLM line to a full commercial frontier platform and one of China’s designated “AI tiger” companies.
events.reaction: Domestic benchmarks and a low-cost Flash tier drove adoption, while U.S. observers increasingly treated Zhipu as a strategic—not merely commercial—competitor.
events.lost: Baidu/Alibaba’s unchallenged domestic platform position and reliance on Western agents.

events.title: Qwen 1.5 scales from 0.5B to 110B and MoE
events.development: Alibaba released Qwen 1.5 across compact, dense, and mixture-of-experts checkpoints, culminating in Qwen1.5-110B; upgraded Qwen-VL Max/Plus served vision users.
events.technicalChange: Native Hugging Face support, stronger multilingual chat, 32K context, quantized variants, and a small sparse MoE made one consistent family deployable from edge devices to servers.
events.meaning: Breadth and tooling, not only a single leaderboard winner, became Qwen’s durable advantage.
events.reaction: Developers praised the permissive releases and size ladder; concerns persisted around licenses for some large variants and Chinese content controls in hosted services.
events.lost: Llama’s default status in non-Western open deployments.

events.title: Bard becomes Gemini; Ultra 1.0 ships in Gemini Advanced
events.development: Google retired the Bard name, released a Gemini mobile app, and put its largest model behind a Google One subscription.
events.technicalChange: Ultra delivered Google’s strongest reasoning, coding, and native multimodal capability, while Nano and Pro covered device and mass-market tiers.
events.meaning: One model brand now spanned consumer assistant, Android, Workspace, and Cloud, correcting Google’s fragmented launch.
events.reaction: Reviewers saw a credible GPT-4 rival but criticized product naming, geographic limits, and image-generation errors that led Google to pause people generation later that month.
events.gained: Gemini as a unified brand and Google subscription distribution.
events.lost: Bard and some trust in Google’s safety/quality tuning.

events.title: Gemini 1.5 Pro and Sora reveal two different scaling frontiers
events.development: Google previewed Gemini 1.5 Pro with a one-million-token context; OpenAI previewed Sora text-to-video.
events.technicalChange: Gemini used a sparse mixture-of-experts architecture and could reason across roughly an hour of video, 11 hours of audio, or huge codebases. Sora treated compressed video patches as tokens in a diffusion Transformer, generating coherent minute-long scenes.
events.meaning: Context and world simulation joined model scale as frontier dimensions.
events.reaction: Gemini’s needle-in-a-haystack demos reset expectations for context; Sora produced awe and immediate deepfake/creative-labor anxiety, though access stayed restricted.
events.gained: Google on long context and OpenAI on generative video narrative.
events.lost: short-context APIs and video startups’ perceived lead.

events.title: Google releases Gemma 2B and 7B open weights
events.development: Google shipped compact models derived from Gemini research with responsible-generation tooling and deployment recipes.
events.technicalChange: Gemma brought a modern decoder architecture, broad tokenizer, safety filtering guidance, and optimized runtimes for laptops, workstations, and cloud GPUs.
events.meaning: Google entered the open-weight contest it had largely ceded to Meta and Mistral and used openness to strengthen JAX, Keras, PyTorch, Hugging Face, and Vertex distribution.
events.reaction: The models were efficient and accessible, but the custom license and small initial sizes limited claims of frontier openness.
events.lost: Meta/Mistral exclusivity over credible open families.

events.title: Mistral Large launches as Microsoft invests
events.development: Mistral released a proprietary flagship through its own platform and Azure while Microsoft took a small equity stake.
events.technicalChange: Mistral Large added strong multilingual reasoning, coding, and native function calling; the Le Chat assistant gave it a consumer interface.
events.meaning: Mistral adopted a dual strategy—permissive small/open models plus paid closed frontier models—and gained hyperscaler distribution.
events.reaction: Europe celebrated a homegrown challenger, but critics questioned whether an Azure deal weakened the case for European strategic autonomy.
events.lost: the expectation that Mistral would remain purely open.

events.title: Claude 3 Opus, Sonnet, and Haiku establish a complete tiered family
events.development: Anthropic released three multimodal models: Opus for maximum intelligence, Sonnet for balance, and Haiku for speed/cost.
events.technicalChange: All accepted images, improved instruction following and refusal calibration, supported 200K context, and used tier-specific latency/economics; Opus led major benchmarks at release.
events.meaning: Anthropic briefly took the perceived frontier lead from GPT-4 and showed that a coherent price/performance ladder was an enterprise advantage.
events.reaction: Opus received exceptional reviews for reasoning and prose; Haiku’s speed made Claude viable for high-volume use.
events.lost: OpenAI’s uncontested quality lead and single-model pricing strategies.

events.title: Taalas emerges with a model-to-silicon thesis
events.development: The Toronto startup disclosed $50 million in funding and a “direct-to-silicon foundry” plan.
events.technicalChange: Instead of a broadly programmable accelerator, Taalas proposed compiling model architecture and weights into hardened silicon, removing HBM weight movement and much control overhead.
events.meaning: It revived extreme specialization as a possible answer to inference cost—accepting model inflexibility in exchange for tokens per watt and per dollar.
events.reaction: Experienced-chip-team credentials generated interest, but 1,000× cost-improvement language was treated as an unproven claim.
events.gained: specialized inference as an investable category.
events.lost: none yet; GPUs retained the flexibility advantage.

events.title: Devin packages the software-engineering agent
events.development: Cognition previewed Devin as an autonomous software engineer with its own shell, browser, editor, and sandbox.
events.technicalChange: Persistent state, planning, error recovery, and an integrated execution environment let one model attempt thousands of steps and submit completed work rather than suggestions.
events.meaning: Coding assistants moved from inline completion toward asynchronous delegation; SWE-bench became a commercial benchmark.
events.reaction: The 13.86% unassisted SWE-bench claim and polished demos went viral, followed by scrutiny of task selection, failures, and the “replace engineers” framing.
events.lost: completion-only coding tools and confidence in demos without reproducible traces.

events.title: Cerebras WSE-3 doubles wafer-scale performance
events.development: Cerebras introduced the 5-nanometer WSE-3 and CS-3 system.
events.technicalChange: One wafer carried four trillion transistors, 900,000 cores, 44 GB on-chip SRAM, and a claimed 125 petaflops, scaling to 2,048 systems without conventional GPU model partitioning.
events.meaning: Cerebras remained the most radical shipped alternative to GPU clusters and built a path from training toward ultra-fast inference.
events.reaction: The specifications drew renewed respect, while customer concentration, proprietary software, and NVIDIA ecosystem risk constrained adoption.
events.gained: Cerebras and G42’s Condor Galaxy installations.
events.lost: the presumption that package-level chiplets were the only manufacturable scale strategy.

events.title: NVIDIA Blackwell turns the rack into the computer
events.development: NVIDIA announced B100/B200, the GB200 Grace Blackwell Superchip, and liquid-cooled GB200 NVL72 systems.
events.technicalChange: Two reticle-limited dies acted as one GPU over a 10 TB/s link; FP4 Tensor Cores, fifth-generation NVLink, 192 GB HBM3e per B200, RAS engines, decompression, and 800 Gb/s Quantum-X/Spectrum-X networking targeted trillion-parameter inference.
events.meaning: NVIDIA’s unit of competition moved from a chip to a 72-GPU rack and full “AI factory,” increasing customer dependence on its networking, CPUs, software, and thermal design.
events.reaction: Demand was immediate, though heat, liquid cooling, packaging yield, and rollout delays raised deployment risk.
events.gained: NVIDIA, TSMC CoWoS, HBM, power/cooling suppliers.
events.lost: merchant component modularity and smaller infrastructure buyers.

events.title: Microsoft hires Inflection’s founders and licenses its models
events.development: Mustafa Suleyman, Karén Simonyan, and most of Inflection’s staff joined a new Microsoft AI organization; Microsoft paid for model access while Inflection continued under new leadership.
events.technicalChange: No public architecture leap—the innovation was a transaction that transferred scarce talent and IP without a conventional acquisition.
events.meaning: “Reverse acquihires” became a method for hyperscalers to absorb frontier teams while attempting to avoid full merger review.
events.reaction: The deal was seen as a rescue for Inflection investors and a warning to standalone labs; U.S. and U.K. regulators examined it.
events.lost: Inflection’s independence and investors’ original product thesis.

events.title: The U.N. General Assembly adopts its first AI resolution
events.development: Member states unanimously backed a U.S.-led resolution on safe, secure, trustworthy AI and equitable access.
events.technicalChange: The nonbinding text called for human-rights safeguards, capacity building, interoperable standards, and closing digital divides.
events.meaning: Global AI governance broadened beyond frontier-risk clubs to development, inclusion, and rights—priorities of countries without giant compute clusters.
events.reaction: Consensus was welcomed as a diplomatic baseline; the lack of enforcement and military-AI coverage limited practical effect.
events.gained: U.N. legitimacy and Global South demands.
events.lost: the idea that a handful of frontier states could define the whole agenda.

sources.label: United Nations resolution coverage and text

events.title: DBRX and Jamba expand open architecture choices
events.development: Databricks released DBRX, a 132B/36B-active MoE, and AI21 released Jamba, a 52B/12B-active hybrid Transformer–Mamba model with 256K context.
events.technicalChange: DBRX used fine-grained expert routing and enterprise-oriented data governance; Jamba alternated attention and state-space layers to reduce KV-cache memory while retaining tool-friendly Transformer behavior.
events.meaning: Architecture exploration moved beyond dense Transformers, and enterprise vendors used open weights to drive platforms.
events.reaction: Both were praised as technically bold; serving complexity and weaker ecosystem support limited immediate displacement of Llama/Mixtral.
events.lost: architectural monoculture.

events.title: TSMC expands Arizona and wins proposed CHIPS support
events.development: TSMC raised planned Arizona investment above $65 billion, added a third leading-edge fab, and reached terms for up to $6.6 billion in direct CHIPS funding plus loans.
events.technicalChange: Plans extended the site from N4 to 3 nm and 2 nm-class production, though advanced packaging still largely remained in Taiwan at this stage.
events.meaning: The United States bought partial geographic resilience in the foundry layer on which NVIDIA, AMD, Apple, and custom AI chips depended.
events.reaction: Policymakers celebrated; skeptics noted higher U.S. costs, workforce challenges, and a multiyear timetable.
events.lost: some—though far from all—Taiwan-only concentration risk.

events.title: Llama 3 raises the open-weight baseline
events.development: Meta released 8B and 70B pretrained and instruction-tuned models, with larger variants promised.
events.technicalChange: More than 15 trillion training tokens, a 128K-token vocabulary, grouped-query attention, improved filtering, and extensive preference data produced strong efficiency and instruction following; initial context was 8K.
events.meaning: Meta’s distribution across clouds, hardware, and repositories made Llama a de facto open ecosystem standard.
events.reaction: Developers praised 70B quality and 8B local usability, while the custom license and undisclosed data remained concerns.
events.gained: Meta, open fine-tuners, and inference hosts.
events.lost: smaller open families that could not match distribution.

events.title: TSMC unveils A16 and System-on-Wafer
events.development: TSMC announced a 2026 A16 process and wafer-scale system integration.
events.technicalChange: A16 combined gate-all-around nanosheet transistors with backside “Super Power Rail,” promising 8–10% higher speed or 15–20% lower power than N2P and better density for data-center chips; SoW extended integration beyond conventional packages.
events.meaning: Foundry roadmaps were increasingly shaped by AI power delivery, chiplets, and system scale rather than smartphone logic alone.
events.reaction: Customers saw an answer to Intel’s backside-power pitch and escalating accelerator size; execution and packaging capacity remained the bottlenecks.
events.lost: Intel Foundry’s differentiation and designers without access to leading packaging slots.

events.title: DeepSeek-V2 attacks the cost structure
events.development: DeepSeek released a 236B-parameter, 21B-active MoE model and dramatically cut its API price.
events.technicalChange: Multi-head Latent Attention compressed keys/values and DeepSeekMoE routed fine-grained shared/specialized experts; the team reported 42.5% lower training cost, 93.3% smaller KV cache, and up to 5.76× generation throughput versus its predecessor.
events.meaning: Memory engineering and sparse activation—not privileged access to the newest chips—could reset both training and serving economics. A domestic Chinese price war followed.
events.reaction: Initially underappreciated outside China, V2 became the architectural foundation for the V3/R1 shock.
events.gained: DeepSeek, efficient open models, API buyers.
events.lost: high-margin Chinese model APIs and dense-model assumptions.

events.title: GPT-4o makes multimodality native and real time
events.development: OpenAI released “omni,” a single model for text, vision, and audio, initially with text/image outputs and staged voice/video rollout.
events.technicalChange: It processed and generated modalities end to end instead of chaining speech recognition, text reasoning, and speech synthesis; audio response averaged 320 ms. API text was twice as fast, half the price, and rate-limited higher than GPT-4 Turbo.
events.meaning: Latency, prosody, interruption, and visual awareness made AI feel like a live collaborator rather than a turn-based chatbot.
events.reaction: The voice demo drew both amazement and comparisons to Her; staged safety review and a voice resembling Scarlett Johansson generated controversy.
events.gained: OpenAI’s consumer product and real-time API.
events.lost: separate speech/vision pipelines and Google’s opportunity to own multimodal assistants.

events.title: Google I/O introduces Gemini 1.5 Flash, Project Astra, Veo, and Trillium TPU
events.development: Google released a distilled low-latency Flash model, improved 1.5 Pro, previewed a two-million-token window, showed the live multimodal Astra assistant, unveiled Veo video generation, and announced sixth-generation Trillium TPU.
events.technicalChange: Flash optimized high-volume serving; Astra streamed audio/video with memory; Trillium delivered a claimed 4.7× per-chip compute gain and stronger interconnect/memory.
events.meaning: Google’s answer was full-stack and visibly productized, spanning models, agents, media, search, devices, and silicon.
events.reaction: The breadth restored confidence, though many features were previews and naming remained complex.
events.lost: the narrative that it had permanently missed the generative-AI transition.

events.title: EU Council gives final approval to the AI Act
events.development: Member states completed the legislative process after Parliament’s March vote.
events.technicalChange: The final text established risk tiers, banned selected uses, mandated transparency for chatbots/deepfakes, and imposed special duties on general-purpose models and those above a systemic-risk compute threshold.
events.meaning: Model providers now had a multiyear compliance calendar with fines tied to global turnover.
events.reaction: Supporters called it the first comprehensive AI law; business groups worried Europe would regulate a technology it did not lead.
events.gained: the EU AI Office, auditors, rights claimants.
events.lost: un documented high-risk deployers; EU startups potentially bore disproportionate fixed costs.

sources.label: Council of the EU final approval

events.title: Seoul summit turns frontier safety into company commitments
events.development: Sixteen companies, including U.S., Chinese, European, and Middle Eastern developers, promised safety frameworks, external evaluation, security, and release thresholds by the 2025 summit.
events.technicalChange: Firms committed to define intolerable-risk boundaries and, if mitigations failed, not develop or deploy a model.
events.meaning: Bletchley’s principles acquired company-specific implementation deadlines, though still without binding sanctions.
events.reaction: Cross-border participation was welcomed; skeptics questioned self-defined thresholds and whether commercial competition would override them.
events.lost: a small amount of labs’ unilateral release discretion.

events.title: Qwen2 broadens languages, sizes, and context
events.development: Alibaba released dense 0.5B–72B and sparse 57B-A14B models.
events.technicalChange: Training expanded beyond Chinese/English to 27 additional languages, with grouped-query attention, improved coding/math, and up to 128K context in selected variants.
events.meaning: Qwen shifted from a Chinese-language alternative to a global open foundation family competitive with Llama and Mistral.
events.reaction: The 72B model gained broad adoption and fine-tunes; U.S. policy concerns did little to slow open-weight downloads.
events.lost: Western families’ language and ecosystem lead.

events.title: Apple Intelligence pairs on-device models with ChatGPT
events.development: Apple announced system-level writing, image, notification, and Siri features, using private cloud compute for larger tasks and optional GPT-4o for requests Apple’s models could not handle.
events.technicalChange: Routing, on-device inference, privacy attestations, and permissioned external-model handoff became part of the consumer AI stack.
events.meaning: OpenAI gained access to Apple’s device distribution without becoming the default for every task; Apple admitted it needed a frontier partner.
events.reaction: Privacy architecture was praised, while the delayed rollout and modest Siri capability fed concern that Apple lagged.
events.gained: OpenAI distribution and Apple’s privacy differentiation.
events.lost: Google’s default-assistant advantage and Apple’s aura of self-sufficiency.

events.title: Claude 3.5 Sonnet and Artifacts outperform at the middle tier
events.development: Anthropic released Claude 3.5 Sonnet at the price and speed of Claude 3 Sonnet while surpassing Opus on many evaluations; Artifacts displayed code, documents, and designs beside chat.
events.technicalChange: Coding, visual reasoning, instruction following, and humor improved, while the artifact workspace created an iterative UI above the model.
events.meaning: A mid-priced model could obsolete a premium flagship, and editable outputs became as important as conversational responses.
events.reaction: Developers rapidly made Sonnet a coding favorite; Artifacts previewed the shift from chat to software creation.
events.lost: Claude 3 Opus, GPT-4-class price premiums, and plain chat interfaces.

events.title: Gemma 2 brings stronger small and mid-size open models
events.development: Google released 9B and 27B variants, later adding 2B.
events.technicalChange: Sliding-window/global attention interleaving, knowledge distillation, logit soft-capping, and extensive safety evaluations let 27B compete with models more than twice its size and 9B serve efficiently on limited hardware.
events.meaning: Distillation from proprietary teachers became a standard route to compact quality.
events.reaction: Developers praised performance-per-parameter; the Gemma license still prevented full open-source classification.
events.lost: larger open models whose quality no longer justified serving cost.

events.title: Llama 3.1 405B becomes the first broadly available frontier-scale open weight
events.development: Meta released 8B, 70B, and 405B models with 128K context, eight languages, and tool use.
events.technicalChange: The dense 405B model trained on more than 15 trillion tokens using over 16,000 H100s; Meta used FP8 inference and generated synthetic data for smaller models.
events.meaning: Developers could distill, fine-tune, and self-host a model competitive with leading closed APIs, while clouds and NVIDIA monetized deployment.
events.reaction: It was hailed as a milestone for open access, alongside criticism of the license, safety risk, and enormous serving requirements.
events.lost: closed labs’ exclusive access to frontier-class weights.

events.title: Mistral Large 2 and specialist models diversify the family
events.development: Mistral launched a 123B flagship with 128K context after releasing Codestral, Mathstral, Codestral Mamba, and the 12B Mistral NeMo.
events.technicalChange: Large 2 emphasized multilingual code, function calling, and concise responses; specialists tested code licensing, state-space architecture, math post-training, and a new tokenizer.
events.meaning: Mistral competed through a portfolio and architecture experimentation rather than one general model.
events.reaction: Quality was strong, but noncommercial research licenses on the largest/specialist weights complicated its “open European champion” image.
events.lost: license simplicity and some open-source goodwill.

events.title: The EU AI Act enters into force
events.development: The final regulation became law, starting a staged application through 2027 and beyond.
events.technicalChange: Prohibited practices would apply in six months, general-purpose-model duties after one year, and most other rules after two years, backed by an AI Office and national authorities.
events.meaning: Providers needed training-data summaries, copyright policies, technical documentation, evaluations, security, and incident processes on an enforceable schedule.
events.reaction: Compliance programs accelerated; debate shifted from whether the law would pass to how the Commission would define systemic models and codes.
events.gained: EU rulemaking and large providers able to absorb compliance.
events.lost: opaque release processes and Europe’s fastest-moving startups at the margin.

sources.label: European Commission: AI Act enters into force

events.title: Qwen2-Audio unifies audio analysis and voice chat
events.development: Alibaba released base and instruction-tuned audio-language models.
events.technicalChange: One model handled speech, natural sounds, music, and audio events, with an audio-analysis mode and direct voice-chat mode rather than requiring a separate speech recognizer.
events.meaning: Native audio competition widened beyond GPT-4o and Gemini, with open weights enabling research and local adaptation.
events.reaction: The release reinforced Qwen’s multimodal breadth, though real-time product quality still favored closed systems.
events.lost: modular ASR-plus-LLM stacks’ exclusivity.

events.title: Cerebras and Groq make token speed a product category
events.development: Cerebras opened WSE-3-based inference, claiming 1,800 tokens/s for Llama 3.1 8B and 450 tokens/s for 70B; Groq’s deterministic LPU cloud had already popularized near-instant open-model responses.
events.technicalChange: Both reduced the memory-movement and scheduling overhead that makes GPU autoregressive decode latency-bound—Cerebras with wafer-scale SRAM/bandwidth, Groq with compiler-scheduled tensor streaming.
events.meaning: Per-user latency became a strategic dimension for voice, reasoning loops, and agents, not just aggregate throughput.
events.reaction: Demos felt qualitatively different; questions focused on economics at utilization, model coverage, and vendor benchmark comparability.
events.lost: the assumption that optimized GPUs would own every serving workload.

events.title: OpenAI o1 makes test-time reasoning the new scaling axis
events.development: OpenAI released o1-preview and the smaller o1-mini.
events.technicalChange: Large-scale reinforcement learning trained the models to spend variable compute on an internal chain of thought before answering, improving math, science, coding, and planning as inference time increased.
events.meaning: The frontier shifted from predicting better immediately to thinking longer, expanding demand for inference compute and changing model evaluation.
events.reaction: Olympiad-style results drew excitement, while slow responses, high prices, missing tools, hidden reasoning, and simple-task regressions produced caution.
events.gained: OpenAI, RL post-training, and inference suppliers.
events.lost: conventional next-token chat models and parameter count as the only scaling story.

events.title: Qwen2.5 releases a broad specialist model matrix
events.development: Alibaba released general 0.5B–72B models plus Qwen2.5-Coder and Qwen2.5-Math variants.
events.technicalChange: Up to 18 trillion pretraining tokens, improved structured-data/JSON output, 128K context in major variants, and domain-specific training strengthened coding and math.
events.meaning: Open models became product families with specialist routes, not one checkpoint expected to do everything.
events.reaction: Qwen2.5 rapidly became a preferred base for fine-tuning and later reasoning distillation.
events.gained: Alibaba and derivative-model builders, including DeepSeek distills.
events.lost: smaller Western open families and generic-only releases.

events.title: Llama 3.2 adds vision and phone-scale models
events.development: Meta released 11B/90B vision-language models and 1B/3B text models for edge devices.
events.technicalChange: Vision adapters aligned an image encoder with the language model, while compact text models targeted on-device summarization, rewriting, and tool use.
events.meaning: Meta used open weights and hardware partnerships to push a cloud-to-edge platform, reducing dependence on Apple/Google model APIs.
events.reaction: Device models were welcomed; the vision weights’ exclusion from the EU because of regulatory uncertainty dramatized jurisdictional fragmentation.
events.gained: Meta’s on-device ecosystem and Qualcomm/MediaTek partners.
events.lost: cloud-only model strategies and EU access to one launch.

events.title: California vetoes SB 1047
events.development: Governor Gavin Newsom vetoed a bill that would have imposed safety plans, shutdown capability, reporting, and liability-related duties on developers of very large models.
events.technicalChange: The bill used training-compute/cost thresholds as a regulatory proxy; the veto argued that risk depends on deployment and capability, not model size alone.
events.meaning: The leading U.S. AI state declined the first strong frontier-model statute while commissioning a more evidence-based framework.
events.reaction: Major labs and venture groups welcomed the veto; safety researchers and some Anthropic voices saw a lost chance for enforceable guardrails.
events.gained: frontier labs and California’s innovation-first coalition.
