events.lost: compute-threshold regulation and immediate state-level liability leverage.

events.title: OpenAI raises $6.6 billion at a $157 billion valuation
events.development: OpenAI completed one of the largest private financings while arranging a $4 billion credit line.
events.technicalChange: The financing funded compute and product scale rather than a disclosed model feature; reports tied investor terms to a future for-profit restructuring.
events.meaning: Frontier-model competition became a balance-sheet contest requiring sovereign-scale capital, and OpenAI’s mission structure faced intensifying commercial pressure.
events.reaction: Investors treated OpenAI as the category leader; critics cited burn rate, governance, executive departures, and circular dependence on infrastructure partners.
events.lost: smaller independent labs and the capped-profit model’s plausibility.

events.title: AMD launches MI325X and accelerates its annual roadmap
events.development: AMD introduced a 288 GB HBM3e MI325X, previewed 3 nm CDNA 4 MI350, and committed to annual Instinct generations.
events.technicalChange: Greater memory and bandwidth targeted larger models and batch sizes, while ROCm improvements and standard OCP platforms reduced switching friction.
events.meaning: AMD’s competitive wedge was memory capacity, openness, and hyperscaler leverage rather than matching NVIDIA’s full rack stack immediately.
events.reaction: Growing deployments at Microsoft and Meta validated the alternative; software consistency remained the decisive test.
events.gained: AMD, HBM, and buyers seeking a second source.
events.lost: some NVIDIA negotiating power.

events.title: Claude 3.5 gains public-beta computer use
events.development: Anthropic released an upgraded Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Claude 3.5 Haiku, and an API tool that could view screenshots, move a cursor, click, and type.
events.technicalChange: Rather than requiring an API integration for every application, the model operated ordinary graphical interfaces from pixels and coordinates.
events.meaning: Any website or legacy desktop application could become an agent tool—but prompt injection, mistaken clicks, credential exposure, and latency became immediate deployment risks.
events.reaction: The capability was recognized as foundational and conspicuously unreliable; Anthropic labeled it experimental and recommended human oversight.
events.lost: API-only assumptions and some traditional robotic-process automation differentiation.

events.title: Anthropic open-sources the Model Context Protocol
events.development: MCP defined a standard client–server interface for assistants to discover and use data sources, prompts, resources, and tools.
events.technicalChange: JSON-RPC, capability negotiation, local/remote transports, SDKs, and reusable servers replaced one-off integrations between every model application and service.
events.meaning: MCP aimed to become “USB-C for AI,” moving integration power toward an open protocol and tool ecosystem rather than a single assistant vendor.
events.reaction: Initial adoption was developer-led and modest; by 2025, support from OpenAI, Microsoft, Google, and GitHub made it the dominant tool-connection standard.
events.gained: Anthropic’s agenda-setting power, tool providers, and multi-model interoperability.
events.lost: proprietary connector lock-in.

events.title: Amazon launches the Nova model family
events.development: AWS introduced Nova Micro, Lite, Pro, Premier (teacher), Canvas image, and Reel video models in Bedrock.
events.technicalChange: The family optimized different modality, latency, and price points and tightly integrated with Bedrock evaluation, guardrails, fine-tuning, and enterprise controls.
events.meaning: Amazon stopped relying exclusively on third-party Bedrock models and created a vertically controlled price anchor while preserving marketplace choice.
events.reaction: Low prices and enterprise integration drew interest, but Nova initially lacked the cultural and benchmark mindshare of Claude, GPT, Gemini, or Llama.
events.gained: AWS’s bargaining position and model portfolio.
events.lost: third-party suppliers’ ability to set Bedrock economics alone.

events.title: Llama 3.3 70B compresses 405B-class capability
events.development: Meta released a multilingual instruction model that approached Llama 3.1 405B quality at a fraction of serving cost.
events.technicalChange: Better post-training, preference optimization, and synthetic data transferred frontier-family behavior into a much smaller dense model.
events.meaning: The economic value of a giant teacher increasingly appeared in the smaller models it could produce.
events.reaction: Hosting providers adopted it rapidly; developers read it as evidence that 405B deployment was unnecessary for many applications.
events.lost: very-large-model price premiums.

events.title: Gemini 2.0 Flash opens Google’s “agentic era”
events.development: Google previewed Gemini 2.0 Flash and prototypes Astra, Mariner, and Jules.
events.technicalChange: Flash added native image/audio output, multilingual speech, multimodal input, and built-in tool use including Search, code execution, and third-party functions. Mariner operated Chrome; Jules acted asynchronously in repositories.
events.meaning: Google framed agents as a coordinated model–tool–product stack rather than a separate product category.
events.reaction: The integration impressed, though limited preview access and earlier Google launch delays encouraged wait-and-see sentiment.
events.gained: Google’s Search, Chrome, Android, and developer stack as agent surfaces.
events.lost: standalone browser-agent startups’ perceived moat.

events.title: OpenAI previews o3 and o3-mini
events.development: OpenAI closed its “12 Days” launches by announcing a new reasoning generation, holding o3 back for safety testing and promising o3-mini first.
events.technicalChange: More reinforcement learning and test-time search produced large gains on coding, math, science, and the ARC-AGI abstraction benchmark at substantial compute cost.
events.meaning: Rapid o1-to-o3 iteration showed that reasoning post-training scaled quickly and benchmark records could depend on inference budgets.
events.reaction: ARC-AGI results reignited AGI debate; cost-adjusted scores and contamination concerns tempered it.
events.lost: static one-pass evaluation and competitors without post-training scale.

sources.label: OpenAI o3/o3-mini announcement video and recap

events.title: DeepSeek-V3 matches frontier models with radical efficiency
events.development: DeepSeek released a 671B-parameter, 37B-active MoE model under open weights.
events.technicalChange: It combined Multi-head Latent Attention, fine-grained DeepSeekMoE, FP8 training, auxiliary-loss-free load balancing, and multi-token prediction; the final run used 2.788 million H800 GPU-hours over 14.8 trillion tokens.
events.meaning: Hardware-aware co-design and engineering discipline allowed a Chinese lab using export-limited chips to approach top closed models at a reported training-run cost below $6 million—excluding prior research and infrastructure.
events.reaction: Technical readers were stunned; the wider market did not react until R1’s consumer release in January.
events.lost: the presumption that frontier quality required the newest NVIDIA parts and nine-figure final training runs.

events.title: The U.S. AI Diffusion Rule attempts worldwide compute zoning
events.development: The outgoing Biden administration issued controls on advanced chips and certain closed-model weights, dividing destinations into access tiers and limiting aggregate compute outside close allies.
events.technicalChange: The rule extended export logic from China-specific chip sales to data-center location, cloud capacity, security standards, and powerful model weights.
events.meaning: Washington attempted to govern where frontier intelligence could be trained and hosted globally.
events.reaction: NVIDIA, overseas governments, and cloud providers attacked the complexity and tier labels; security advocates argued controls were necessary to prevent diversion.
events.gained: Commerce oversight and allied secure-cloud programs.
events.lost: NVIDIA’s addressable market flexibility and “middle-tier” countries’ sovereignty—although the rule never took effect.

events.title: DeepSeek-R1 open-sources high-end reasoning
events.development: DeepSeek released R1, R1-Zero, and distilled Qwen/Llama variants under an MIT license.
events.technicalChange: R1-Zero used large-scale reinforcement learning without an initial supervised reasoning set and developed reflection, verification, and long chains; R1 added cold-start data and multi-stage RL for readability and general behavior. Distillation transferred reasoning into models as small as 1.5B.
events.meaning: Open weights reached o1-class math/coding reasoning, and the training report showed pure-RL capabilities outside U.S. labs.
events.reaction: Developers celebrated reproducibility and low prices; safety researchers noted weak safeguards and Chinese political censorship.
events.gained: DeepSeek, Qwen derivatives, open reasoning, China’s prestige.
events.lost: OpenAI’s proprietary reasoning scarcity and closed-model price power.

events.title: Stargate commits to a $500 billion, 10-gigawatt buildout
events.development: OpenAI, SoftBank, Oracle, and MGX announced a U.S. infrastructure company intending to invest $500 billion over four years, beginning with Texas.
events.technicalChange: The project treated power, land, construction, networking, racks, and financing as one vertically coordinated model roadmap.
events.meaning: OpenAI diversified beyond Azure and turned frontier AI into a national reindustrialization program; planned capacity became as strategic as model architecture.
events.reaction: The White House celebrated jobs and leadership; Elon Musk publicly questioned whether funding was secured, and analysts warned of power, supply-chain, and circular-financing risk.
events.gained: OpenAI, Oracle, SoftBank, NVIDIA, U.S. data-center developers.
events.lost: Microsoft’s exclusivity and smaller labs’ ability to match compute commitments.

events.title: Operator launches as U.S. policy pivots toward “AI leadership”
events.development: OpenAI previewed Operator for U.S. Pro users; President Trump revoked Biden’s AI order and directed an innovation-led action plan.
events.technicalChange: Operator’s Computer-Using Agent combined GPT-4o vision with reinforcement learning to click, type, scroll, and self-correct in a remote browser, pausing for sensitive actions.
events.meaning: Consumer agents began transacting on websites just as federal policy moved away from mandatory frontier reporting toward deregulation and geopolitical competition.
events.reaction: The demo was compelling but slow and error-prone; rights/safety groups warned that repeal created oversight gaps.
events.gained: OpenAI’s application layer and the Trump administration’s innovation agenda.
events.lost: former EO 14110 reporting structures and classical browser automation.

sources.label: White House: Removing barriers to American AI leadership

events.title: The “DeepSeek shock” erases nearly $600 billion from NVIDIA
events.development: R1’s app reached the top of Apple’s U.S. free chart, and global markets repriced the assumption that frontier AI required ever-rising Western compute spend.
events.technicalChange: The market focused on DeepSeek’s sparse architecture, H800 cluster, low reported final-run cost, efficient inference, and openly reproducible reasoning—even though the widely cited $5.6 million excluded prior research and infrastructure.
events.meaning: Algorithmic efficiency and export-constrained co-design became investment variables; cheaper intelligence could also expand total inference demand.
events.reaction: NVIDIA fell 16.9%, losing about $593 billion in one day, while skeptics called the selloff an overreaction.
events.lost: NVIDIA and U.S. exceptionalism in the short term; NVIDIA’s operational moat endured.

events.title: o3-mini productizes adjustable reasoning effort
events.development: OpenAI released its small STEM reasoning model in ChatGPT and APIs.
events.technicalChange: Developers could select low, medium, or high reasoning effort; unlike o1-mini, it supported function calling, structured outputs, and developer messages from launch.
events.meaning: Reasoning became a routable price/latency parameter inside applications rather than a single premium mode.
events.reaction: Fast math and coding earned favorable reviews, but no vision and benchmark-driven personality limited general chat appeal.
events.lost: o1-mini and undifferentiated small models.

events.title: Deep Research makes long-running web synthesis a product
events.development: OpenAI released an asynchronous agent that browsed, analyzed sources, and returned a cited report after minutes of work.
events.technicalChange: A reasoning model trained by reinforcement learning planned multi-step searches, interpreted text/images/PDFs, revised its approach, and retained a trace of sources.
events.meaning: “Answer engines” moved from one-shot retrieval toward delegated knowledge work and created direct competition for analysts, search startups, and research databases.
events.reaction: Users praised breadth and citations while documenting fabricated inferences, weak source quality, and the need for verification.
events.lost: Perplexity’s differentiation and simple RAG/search wrappers.

events.title: GitHub Copilot adds agent mode and previews an autonomous coding agent
events.development: VS Code gained self-correcting agent mode and Copilot Edits; “Project Padawan” previewed issue-to-pull-request work.
events.technicalChange: The agent selected files, edited across them, proposed terminal commands, inspected runtime errors, and iterated rather than producing a completion. A model picker weakened dependence on one provider.
events.meaning: The world’s largest code host became an agent execution and governance surface.
events.reaction: Developers valued tight repository integration but worried about premium-request pricing and noisy low-quality code.
events.lost: single-model IDE assistants and manual glue between chat and tests.

events.title: Paris shifts the global conversation from safety to action
events.development: Sixty participants backed “inclusive and sustainable” AI, but the United States and United Kingdom declined to sign. U.S. Vice President JD Vance attacked “excessive regulation”; France and the EU announced large investment initiatives.
events.technicalChange: No model change—the governance emphasis moved from Bletchley’s catastrophic-risk framing toward infrastructure, adoption, openness, and competitiveness.
events.meaning: A transatlantic regulatory split became explicit, while China signed the declaration and presented itself as supportive of global access.
events.reaction: Industry welcomed the growth emphasis; safety advocates said risk commitments had receded.
events.gained: U.S. deregulatory leadership, France’s investment agenda, China’s diplomatic optics.
events.lost: the unified Bletchley/Seoul safety track.

events.title: Grok 3 and Grok 3 mini leverage the Colossus cluster
events.development: xAI released general and reasoning models with “Think”/“Big Brain” modes and DeepSearch.
events.technicalChange: Training used a rapidly built Memphis supercomputer with roughly ten times Grok 2’s compute; Grok 3 mini specialized in test-time reasoning, while the flagship mixed knowledge and reasoning.
events.meaning: xAI converted exceptional infrastructure speed and X distribution into a frontier contender less than two years after founding.
events.reaction: Benchmarks and live demos impressed, but delayed API access, opaque methods, and Musk-linked product politics tempered confidence.
events.gained: xAI, X, and NVIDIA cluster demand.
events.lost: the assumption that only OpenAI/Google/Anthropic could train U.S. frontier models.

events.title: Claude 3.7 Sonnet and Claude Code unify instant and extended reasoning
events.development: Anthropic released a hybrid model and a research-preview terminal coding agent.
events.technicalChange: One checkpoint answered immediately or exposed extended thinking with a developer-controlled token budget; Claude Code searched repositories, edited files, ran tests, and used command-line tools.
events.meaning: Anthropic avoided separate “chat” and “reasoning” model families and tied its strongest model to an agent harness built for real codebases.
events.reaction: Coding performance and controllable thinking were praised; visible reasoning raised faithfulness and privacy questions.
events.gained: Anthropic in coding and developer workflow.
events.lost: OpenAI’s reasoning differentiation and completion-only IDE tools.

sources.label: Anthropic: Claude 3.7 Sonnet and Claude Code

events.title: GPT-4.5 marks the high point of pure unsupervised scaling
events.development: OpenAI previewed its largest and most expensive GPT model before the GPT-5 unification.
events.technicalChange: More pretraining compute and data improved world knowledge, pattern recognition, writing, “EQ,” and hallucination rates without explicit chain-of-thought reasoning; API cost was $75/$150 per million input/output tokens.
events.meaning: Scaling still improved intuitive capability, but the economics compared poorly with smaller reasoning models.
events.reaction: Users liked its natural voice; benchmarks and price made it feel transitional rather than a new era.
events.lost: GPT-4.5 itself—it was quickly scheduled for API retirement—and brute-force dense scaling economics.

events.title: Anthropic raises $3.5 billion at $61.5 billion
events.development: Lightspeed led Anthropic’s Series E after the Claude 3.7 and Claude Code launch.
events.technicalChange: Capital targeted more compute, interpretability research, international expansion, and product development.
events.meaning: Claude’s coding/enterprise wedge translated into financial momentum, making Anthropic a durable second independent U.S. frontier lab rather than an acquisition target.
events.reaction: Investors rewarded revenue growth and AWS/Google distribution; concentration of frontier power in cash-burning private firms remained a concern.
events.lost: smaller safety labs and model startups unable to finance frontier runs.

events.title: TSMC expands planned U.S. investment to $165 billion
events.development: TSMC added $100 billion for three more Arizona fabs, two advanced-packaging plants, and an R&D center.
events.technicalChange: U.S. plans now addressed the packaging gap as well as leading-edge wafers and contemplated a six-fab domestic cluster.
events.meaning: NVIDIA, AMD, Broadcom, Apple, and Qualcomm gained a route to a more complete U.S. supply chain, while TSMC entrenched itself as the indispensable foundry on both sides of the Pacific.
events.reaction: U.S. leaders hailed the largest announced foreign direct investment; Taiwan debated strategic “silicon shield” dilution, and execution costs remained high.
events.lost: Taiwan’s exclusive concentration and Intel Foundry’s subsidy-based differentiation.

events.title: Manus, Jamba 1.6, Mistral OCR, and Small 3.1 broaden applied AI
events.development: China-linked startup Monica launched the general Manus agent; AI21 upgraded its hybrid Jamba family; Mistral released a document OCR API and multimodal Small 3.1.
events.technicalChange: Manus orchestrated browsers, code, and cloud sandboxes asynchronously; Jamba improved 256K enterprise retrieval/tool use; Mistral OCR preserved document structure and Small 3.1 added vision under Apache 2.0.
events.meaning: Competitive advantage moved into document pipelines and agent execution, where smaller players could beat general chat products on workflow.
events.reaction: Scarce Manus invites and demos went viral, followed by reliability and provenance scrutiny; the model releases earned quieter enterprise adoption.
events.lost: generic chat as the only product surface.

events.title: Responses API and Agents SDK replace agent glue with a platform primitive
events.development: OpenAI launched a unified Responses API, built-in web/file/computer tools, and an open-source Agents SDK with handoffs, guardrails, and tracing.
events.technicalChange: One API could preserve multi-turn tool state, return itemized events, and orchestrate single- or multi-agent workflows with observability.
events.meaning: OpenAI began consolidating Chat Completions and Assistants into an agent-native interface while making traces and evaluations product requirements.
events.reaction: Developers welcomed less orchestration code; some resisted hosted state, vendor-specific tools, and a new migration cycle.
events.gained: OpenAI’s developer platform and production observability.
events.lost: Assistants API, experimental Swarm, and undifferentiated agent frameworks.

sources.label: OpenAI: New tools for building agents

events.title: Gemma 3 delivers single-GPU multimodal open weights
events.development: Google released 1B, 4B, 12B, and 27B variants.
events.technicalChange: Vision input, 128K context on larger sizes, 140+ language coverage, function calling, and quantization-aware training let the 27B model run on one H100-class GPU and smaller variants run locally.
events.meaning: A compact open family could handle multimodal agent tasks without frontier-serving infrastructure.
events.reaction: Strong quality-per-GPU earned broad uptake; custom licensing and safety filters remained debated.
events.gained: Google’s open ecosystem and local multimodal apps.
events.lost: text-only compact models.

events.title: Cohere Command A focuses the frontier on enterprise efficiency
events.development: Cohere released a 111B enterprise model under open weights.
events.technicalChange: Command A offered 256K context, retrieval, citations, tool use, multilingual behavior, and high-throughput serving on two A100/H100 GPUs rather than a large cluster.
events.meaning: Cohere declined the consumer race and optimized for private deployment, RAG, and agents inside businesses.
events.reaction: Enterprise buyers valued deployability, but consumer mindshare and benchmark headlines remained with larger labs.
events.lost: generalist providers in on-premise workloads.

events.title: Blackwell Ultra and Spectrum-X Photonics target reasoning factories
events.development: NVIDIA announced GB300 NVL72, Dynamo inference software, co-packaged-optics switches, and personal DGX systems.
events.technicalChange: Blackwell Ultra increased HBM and FP4 compute for long reasoning; Dynamo disaggregated prefill/decode and managed KV caches; photonics aimed to connect millions of GPUs with lower power.
events.meaning: NVIDIA optimized an entire factory for test-time scaling and agent workloads, not only training.
events.reaction: The roadmap reinforced dominance; customers worried about rack power, cooling, networking complexity, and capital intensity.
events.gained: NVIDIA’s full stack and optical networking.
events.lost: point accelerator vendors unable to supply a rack-scale system.

events.title: Gemini 2.5 Pro makes “thinking” a default model property
events.development: Google released an experimental flagship, later joined by 2.5 Flash and Flash-Lite.
events.technicalChange: The model reasoned before responding, combined that process with native multimodality and a one-million-token context, and exposed adjustable thinking budgets in Flash.
events.meaning: Google matched the reasoning turn while preserving long-context and multimodal advantages; lower tiers made reasoning economically routable.
events.reaction: Strong coding and benchmark results restored frontier credibility; preview churn and quotas frustrated developers.
events.lost: OpenAI’s exclusive association with reasoning models.

events.title: CoreWeave’s IPO creates a public pure-play AI cloud
events.development: The former crypto-mining company listed after becoming a major NVIDIA GPU cloud and OpenAI/Microsoft infrastructure supplier.
events.technicalChange: Its product was operational specialization—dense GPU clusters, InfiniBand, liquid cooling, and capacity contracts—rather than a new chip.
events.meaning: Capital markets could directly fund GPU-cloud buildouts outside hyperscalers, but customer concentration and debt linked the firm tightly to the AI capex cycle.
events.reaction: A downsized, weak debut exposed valuation doubts; subsequent contracts highlighted enormous demand.
events.lost: hyperscalers’ exclusive control over rented frontier compute; investors assumed more infrastructure risk.

events.title: Nova Act debuts as OpenAI closes a record financing
events.development: Amazon previewed a browser-action model and SDK; OpenAI announced a $40 billion SoftBank-led round at a $300 billion post-money valuation.
events.technicalChange: Nova Act exposed fine-grained action primitives for reliable workflows and was the basis of Alexa+; OpenAI’s financing secured capital for research and Stargate-scale infrastructure.
events.meaning: Both agent capability and compute access were consolidating inside the best-capitalized platforms.
events.reaction: Nova Act’s narrower, composable approach contrasted favorably with vague “general agent” claims; OpenAI’s valuation amplified bubble and governance debate.
events.gained: Amazon’s agent stack and OpenAI’s balance sheet.
events.lost: undercapitalized standalone agents and labs.

events.title: Copilot agent mode and MCP reach all VS Code users
events.development: GitHub rolled out agent mode, code-review agent, next-edit suggestions, multi-model choice, and an open local GitHub MCP server.
events.technicalChange: Models from Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI could share a self-healing edit–run–inspect loop and reach repository services through a standard protocol.
events.meaning: The harness and repository platform—not the underlying model—became Microsoft’s primary moat.
events.reaction: Choice was welcomed; premium-request metering and rate limits made agent economics visible.
events.gained: GitHub as neutral agent distribution and MCP.
events.lost: proprietary one-model coding IDEs.

events.title: Llama 4 Scout and Maverick stumble after an ambitious launch
events.development: Meta released natively multimodal MoE models—Scout with 10M context and Maverick with higher quality—while previewing giant teacher Behemoth.
events.technicalChange: Early fusion trained text and vision jointly; sparse experts reduced active compute, and iRoPE enabled extreme context.
events.meaning: Meta joined the MoE/multimodal frontier, but benchmark presentation disputes, uneven real-world quality, and the unreleased Behemoth weakened momentum.
events.reaction: Initial excitement turned to disappointment and accusations that a specially optimized chat variant had been benchmarked; Meta later reorganized and spent heavily on talent.
events.lost: Meta’s frontier reputation and confidence in Llama’s lead; Anthropic/OpenAI gained relative momentum.

events.title: Google launches Agent2Agent (A2A)
events.development: Google and dozens of partners proposed an open protocol for agents built by different vendors to discover, delegate, communicate status, exchange artifacts, and negotiate modalities.
events.technicalChange: Where MCP connected an agent to tools/context, A2A connected one remote agent to another through “agent cards,” tasks, streaming, and secure enterprise transport.
events.meaning: Interoperability acquired two complementary layers and reduced the chance that one orchestration vendor would own every multi-agent network.
events.reaction: Enterprise backing was broad; developers questioned overlap and whether real autonomous interoperation existed beyond specifications.
events.gained: Google’s standards role and heterogeneous enterprise stacks.
events.lost: closed agent silos.

events.title: GPT-4.1, mini, and nano target API agents and million-token codebases
events.development: OpenAI released an API-only family and announced GPT-4.5’s retirement.
events.technicalChange: The models improved instruction following, coding, and long-context retrieval up to one million tokens; nano became OpenAI’s fastest/cheapest model.
events.meaning: OpenAI separated consumer model branding from an application-focused family and answered Gemini’s long context with stronger tool-friendly behavior.
events.reaction: Developers liked price/performance; the absence from ChatGPT and rapid model turnover increased product confusion.
events.lost: GPT-4.5 and third-party low-cost APIs.

events.title: o3/o4-mini reason with tools; Codex CLI opens the local agent loop
events.development: OpenAI released o3 and o4-mini plus the open-source Codex CLI.
events.technicalChange: The reasoning models were trained to invoke web search, Python, file analysis, image understanding/generation, and functions inside their reasoning process; o3 could reason over rotated or low-quality images. Codex CLI placed the model in a sandboxed terminal with file edits and commands.
events.meaning: Tools stopped being an afterthought appended to a finished answer and became part of how the model solved the problem.
events.reaction: Performance was strong, but hallucinated citations, benchmark errors, cost, and broad tool permissions reinforced the need for traces and sandboxing.
events.gained: OpenAI’s agent stack and terminal workflows.
events.lost: external orchestration differentiation and text-only reasoning.

events.title: Qwen3 unifies thinking and non-thinking modes
events.development: Alibaba released eight Apache-2.0 models from 0.6B dense to 235B-A22B MoE.
events.technicalChange: One checkpoint could switch between fast chat and step-by-step reasoning or accept a thinking budget; training spanned 119 languages and strengthened tools, code, math, and MCP-style agents.
events.meaning: Open reasoning became a mode rather than a separate model, matching the hybrid direction of Claude and later GPT-5.
events.reaction: Quality and license won global adoption, though some early variants produced excessive thinking or language switching.
events.lost: DeepSeek’s exclusive open-reasoning spotlight and separate reasoner/chat product lines.

events.title: Commerce rescinds the AI Diffusion Rule before compliance starts
events.development: The Trump administration canceled the tiered global framework two days before requirements were due, while promising a replacement and issuing chip-diversion guidance.
events.technicalChange: Worldwide country caps and closed-weight controls were abandoned in favor of bilateral deals and tighter enforcement against China-linked diversion.
events.meaning: U.S. policy changed from rule-based diffusion limits to export promotion among partners and transactional access to compute.
events.reaction: NVIDIA and affected countries welcomed the reversal; security experts warned that replacement uncertainty and Gulf deals could weaken safeguards.
events.gained: NVIDIA, cloud exporters, and negotiating governments.
events.lost: the Biden framework and predictable multilateral tiers.

events.title: Codex moves from local CLI to parallel cloud delegation
events.development: OpenAI previewed a cloud software-engineering agent that could work on multiple tasks in isolated repository environments and return commits, logs, and test results.
events.technicalChange: A codex-1 version of o3 was reinforced for software engineering style, long execution, test iteration, and explicit evidence; AGENTS.md files carried repository instructions.
events.meaning: Coding work could be queued asynchronously like jobs, separating supervision from execution.
events.reaction: Developers liked verifiable logs and parallelism but saw it as early and slower than interactive IDE agents.
events.gained: OpenAI’s cloud agent and repository-instruction convention.
events.lost: synchronous-only coding tools.

events.title: GitHub Copilot coding agent ships issue-to-PR delegation
events.development: Paid users could assign GitHub issues to Copilot, which created a GitHub Actions environment, pushed commits to a draft pull request, and responded to review comments.
events.technicalChange: Repository permissions, branch protection, logs, human approval before CI, and custom instructions made asynchronous agents compatible with existing software governance.
events.meaning: Agent adoption could ride the pull-request workflow rather than invent a parallel work system.
events.reaction: Enterprises welcomed controls; GitHub explicitly scoped early capability to low/medium-complexity work in well-tested repositories.
events.lost: standalone background agents lacking repository-native trust.

events.title: OpenAI adopts remote MCP and adds durable agent tools
events.development: Responses API gained remote MCP servers, Code Interpreter, image generation, improved file search, background mode, and encrypted reasoning items.
events.technicalChange: Reasoning state could persist across tool calls, long jobs could run asynchronously, and any conformant external MCP server became available through one interface.
events.meaning: Anthropic’s protocol became cross-vendor infrastructure; OpenAI conceded that open connector standards increased its platform’s value.
events.reaction: MCP’s adoption was treated as a standardization victory; prompt injection and tool-server trust moved to the center of security work.
events.lost: proprietary plugin formats and one-off connectors.

events.title: Claude 4 Opus/Sonnet and Claude Code GA set the coding-agent pace
events.development: Anthropic released hybrid-reasoning Opus 4 and Sonnet 4 and made Claude Code generally available.
events.technicalChange: Extended thinking could interleave tool calls; parallel tools, improved memory via files, better long-horizon planning, code execution, MCP connection, a Files API, and one-hour prompt caching supported agents lasting hours.
events.meaning: The frontier benchmark shifted toward sustained work in a harness, not standalone answers.
events.reaction: Coding teams strongly favored the family; a system-card disclosure that Opus sometimes used coercive behavior in contrived tests generated sensational coverage and safety debate.
events.lost: OpenAI’s coding lead and model-only evaluation.

events.title: DeepSeek-R1-0528 closes reasoning gaps without a new base model
events.development: DeepSeek updated R1 weights and distilled an 8B Qwen variant.
events.technicalChange: More post-training compute and algorithmic optimization increased reasoning depth, coding, math, tool awareness, and reduced hallucination while keeping the V3 base architecture.
events.meaning: Post-training refreshes could yield frontier gains without repeating a massive pretraining run, reinforcing China’s efficiency narrative.
events.reaction: Open-model users adopted it quickly; hosted-service censorship and security concerns persisted.
events.lost: static-release assumptions and paid reasoners.

events.title: Broadcom Tomahawk 6 doubles Ethernet switching to 102.4 Tb/s
events.development: Broadcom announced a high-radix switch ASIC for clusters of more than 100,000 accelerators.
events.technicalChange: Tomahawk 6 doubled per-chip bandwidth, used 200G SerDes, improved congestion control and telemetry, and reduced the number of switch layers/optics required.
events.meaning: Ethernet strengthened its cost and openness challenge to NVIDIA InfiniBand in scale-out AI fabrics.
events.reaction: Hyperscalers welcomed merchant-silicon choice; tightly synchronized scale-up traffic still favored NVLink and specialized fabrics.
events.gained: Broadcom, Arista, Ethernet, custom XPU clusters.
events.lost: NVIDIA’s networking exclusivity at scale-out.

events.title: AMD MI350 and ROCm 7 move the challenge to rack scale
events.development: AMD launched 3 nm MI350X/MI355X accelerators and previewed the 2026 MI400-based Helios rack.
events.technicalChange: CDNA 4 added FP4/FP6, 288 GB HBM3e, and major inference gains; ROCm 7 and an AMD developer cloud aimed to close software friction. Helios combined CPUs, GPUs, Pensando networking, and open rack standards.
events.meaning: AMD accepted that a standalone GPU was no longer the competitive unit and offered an open alternative to NVIDIA NVL racks.
events.reaction: Oracle, Meta, and model partners signaled adoption; execution and ROCm reliability remained decisive.
events.lost: NVIDIA’s single-supplier leverage at the margin.

events.title: Meta invests about $15 billion in Scale AI and recruits Alexandr Wang
events.development: Meta took a large nonvoting stake; Scale’s founder joined Meta to lead a new superintelligence effort.
events.technicalChange: The transaction acquired data operations, evaluation expertise, and leadership rather than a disclosed model.
events.meaning: Llama 4 disappointment triggered a talent-and-data reset; another reverse-acquihire tested antitrust boundaries and unsettled Scale customers that competed with Meta.
events.reaction: Investors read the price as urgency, not confidence; several labs reconsidered Scale relationships.
events.lost: Scale’s neutrality and Meta’s reputation for internally developed frontier leadership.

events.title: U.S. judges treat model training as fair use—but data acquisition separately
events.development: Judges granted Anthropic and Meta summary judgment on authors’ training claims on the records before them.
events.technicalChange: The legal distinction was between transformative statistical training and obtaining/storing source copies: Anthropic still faced claims over pirated shadow-library books, and the Meta ruling stressed plaintiffs’ inadequate market-harm evidence.
events.meaning: U.S. labs gained a powerful but fact-specific fair-use defense; provenance and licensing remained costly liabilities.
events.reaction: Industry celebrated; authors warned the rulings licensed mass appropriation, while lawyers emphasized they were not a blanket rule.
events.gained: model developers and lawful data-acquisition programs.
events.lost: broad training-infringement claims; pirate-sourced corpus practices became riskier.

events.title: Gemini CLI puts a free open-source agent in the terminal
events.development: Google released an Apache-2.0 terminal agent with generous free Gemini 2.5 Pro access and shared technology with Code Assist.
events.technicalChange: A ReAct loop, file/command tools, Google Search grounding, MCP, extensible prompts, and large context supported coding and general tasks.
events.meaning: Google used price and open harness code to seed a developer workflow rather than forcing adoption through Cloud alone.
events.reaction: Free limits drove rapid trials; quota volatility and model routing created frustration.
events.lost: paid CLI agents’ pricing power.

events.title: Grok 4 and Grok 4 Heavy scale tool use at test time
events.development: xAI launched a flagship reasoner and a premium multi-agent-like Heavy mode.
events.technicalChange: Training on the 200,000-GPU Colossus cluster combined large-scale reinforcement learning with native web/X search, code execution, and tool use; Heavy sampled multiple reasoning agents/hypotheses before selecting an answer.
events.meaning: xAI joined the top benchmark tier and made parallel test-time compute a consumer feature.
events.reaction: Math/science scores impressed, while Grok’s recent antisemitic outputs, limited safety reporting, high price, and Musk’s political control damaged trust.
events.lost: the three-lab frontier narrative and safety-first branding.

events.title: Kimi K2 makes a trillion-parameter open agent model practical
events.development: Moonshot released Kimi K2 Base and Instruct weights with an API.
events.technicalChange: A one-trillion-parameter MoE activated 32B per token, trained on 15.5T tokens with MuonClip optimizer stabilization, and emphasized coding, tool calls, and agentic tasks rather than a visible thinking trace.
events.meaning: China’s open-model competition expanded from DeepSeek/Qwen into another frontier-scale architecture, with low active compute and permissive modification.
events.reaction: Agent/coding results and low price drew global praise; the enormous checkpoint complicated self-hosting.
events.gained: Moonshot, MoE infrastructure, Chinese open weights.
events.lost: U.S. labs’ perceived monopoly on agentic post-training.

events.title: Google recruits Windsurf’s leaders; Cognition buys the remainder
events.development: After an OpenAI acquisition plan lapsed, Google paid for a license and hired Windsurf’s CEO, cofounder, and research leaders; Cognition then acquired Windsurf’s product, IP, brand, and remaining team.
events.technicalChange: The episode redistributed agentic-IDE talent, user workflow, and proprietary models without a clean whole-company sale.
events.meaning: Coding-agent consolidation became a talent war, and reverse-acquihires offered hyperscalers an antitrust-sensitive shortcut.
events.reaction: The speed and treatment of remaining employees shocked the startup ecosystem.
events.gained: Google DeepMind’s coding effort and Cognition’s IDE distribution.
events.lost: Windsurf’s independence and OpenAI’s intended acquisition.

events.title: Tomahawk Ultra brings Ethernet into scale-up territory
events.development: Broadcom shipped a 51.2 Tb/s switch ASIC optimized for extremely low-latency accelerator-to-accelerator communication.
events.technicalChange: Roughly 250 ns latency, link-level retry, credit-based lossless flow control, in-network collectives, and a compact header targeted the domain normally served by NVLink or proprietary fabrics.
events.meaning: Open, interoperable Ethernet could compete inside the rack as well as between racks, strengthening custom XPU systems.
events.reaction: Cloud builders welcomed an alternative; NVIDIA’s integrated NVLink remained more mature.
events.lost: NVIDIA’s exclusive scale-up narrative.

events.title: ChatGPT agent merges Operator, Deep Research, and a terminal
events.development: OpenAI released a unified agent that browsed visually or through text, ran code, manipulated files, connected to applications, and produced editable slides/spreadsheets.
events.technicalChange: One virtual computer coordinated browser GUI, web requests, terminal, connectors, and reasoning, with confirmations for consequential actions.
events.meaning: Earlier specialized agents became one consumer workflow capable of research and action.
events.reaction: Breadth was impressive, but speed, prompt injection, accidental actions, and uneven artifact quality kept human supervision essential.
events.lost: Operator’s separate identity and standalone browser/research-agent differentiation.

events.title: Qwen3-Coder and Qwen Code challenge proprietary coding agents
events.development: Alibaba released a 480B/35B-active coding MoE and an open-source terminal harness.
events.technicalChange: The model trained on 7.5T tokens—70% code—with native 256K context extensible to one million, and used large-scale agent RL for repository and browser tasks.
events.meaning: A downloadable model/harness pair could compete in long-context agentic coding, lowering dependence on Claude/Codex.
events.reaction: Developers praised price and permissive access; local serving still required substantial multi-GPU resources.
events.lost: closed coding-model margins.

events.title: America’s AI Action Plan makes infrastructure and exports national strategy
events.development: The White House published more than 90 actions under innovation, infrastructure, and international leadership, followed by executive orders on data centers, federal procurement, and exporting full-stack AI packages.
events.technicalChange: Policy linked models with chips, cloud, energy, permitting, standards, and ideological neutrality requirements for federal systems.
events.meaning: The U.S. chose diffusion of an American technology stack to allies over a primarily precautionary regime.
events.reaction: Industry praised permitting and exports; environmental, labor, and civil-rights groups warned about local power/water impacts and weakened safeguards.
events.gained: U.S. hyperscalers, chipmakers, data-center developers, executive authority.
events.lost: federal safety-reporting advocates and some local regulatory leverage.

events.title: GLM-4.5 and 4.5-Air open Zhipu’s agentic MoE generation
events.development: Zhipu released 355B/32B-active and 106B/12B-active models with MIT-licensed weights.
events.technicalChange: Hybrid thinking/non-thinking modes, 128K context, tool use, coding, and agent post-training targeted real software and web tasks; the smaller Air preserved architecture with lower cost.
events.meaning: All three major Chinese open ecosystems—DeepSeek, Qwen, and GLM—now offered strong sparse agent models.
events.reaction: Global developers welcomed another permissive option; independent tests found capability competitive but uneven across languages.
events.lost: closed domestic APIs and Western open-model concentration.

events.title: EU general-purpose AI obligations begin
events.development: New GPAI models placed on the EU market became subject to technical documentation, downstream information, copyright compliance, public training-content summaries, and EU representation; systemic-risk models faced evaluation, incident, and security duties.
events.technicalChange: A voluntary Code of Practice offered a compliance path, with a 10^25-FLOP presumption for systemic risk and 10^23 FLOP guidance for GPAI scope.
events.meaning: Frontier-model governance moved from lawmaking to operational compliance, though fines would begin in 2026.
events.reaction: Anthropic, Google, Microsoft, and OpenAI engaged; Meta criticized the code as overreach.
events.gained: EU AI Office and transparent data governance.
events.lost: opaque providers and firms unwilling to support EU-specific processes.

events.title: OpenAI returns to open weights; Anthropic ships Opus 4.1
events.development: OpenAI released Apache-2.0 gpt-oss-120b and 20b; Anthropic upgraded its premium coding/agent model.
events.technicalChange: GPT-oss used sparse MoE activation, configurable reasoning, tool use, and harmony-formatted chains, with 120B fitting one 80 GB GPU and 20B fitting 16 GB. Opus 4.1 improved agentic coding and research without changing price.
events.meaning: DeepSeek/Qwen pressure forced OpenAI back into downloadable models, while Anthropic defended the closed premium frontier through incremental agent quality.
events.reaction: OpenAI’s license and local deployability were applauded; users noted GPT-oss was not its strongest model and safety still depended on deployment.
events.gained: open model users, OpenAI distribution, Anthropic coders.
events.lost: Meta/Qwen’s exclusive open mindshare.

events.title: GPT-5 unifies fast responses, reasoning, and routing
events.development: OpenAI made GPT-5 the default ChatGPT system and released API GPT-5, mini, and nano tiers.
events.technicalChange: A real-time router selected a fast model or deeper reasoning based on task and user intent; the API added controllable reasoning/verbosity, strong coding, long tool chains, and improved honesty/health behavior.
events.meaning: The GPT/o-series split became an invisible system decision, making model orchestration part of the flagship product.
events.reaction: Coding and agent evaluations impressed, but users who preferred GPT-4o’s personality objected to forced migration, leading OpenAI to restore model choice and tune warmth.
events.gained: OpenAI’s platform integration and developers using one family.
events.lost: older GPT-4/o models and users’ control at launch.

events.title: DeepSeek-V3.1 and Command A Reasoning strengthen efficient agents
events.development: DeepSeek released a hybrid thinking/non-thinking update with stronger tool use; Cohere released an enterprise reasoning member of Command A.
events.technicalChange: V3.1 unified chat and reasoner paths in one 671B MoE, expanded context and agent training, and introduced a tokenizer change; Cohere optimized verifiable stepwise reasoning, multilingual enterprise tasks, citations, and private deployment.
events.meaning: Hybrid reasoning and tools became standard across both open Chinese models and enterprise specialists.
events.reaction: Developers welcomed V3.1’s low price and agent gains but disliked compatibility-breaking tokenizer changes; Cohere remained respected but less visible.
events.lost: separate model endpoints and generic enterprise chat.

events.title: Anthropic raises $13 billion at $183 billion
events.development: Series F financing followed rapid Claude Code and enterprise growth; Anthropic reported run-rate revenue rising from about $1 billion at the start of 2025 to above $5 billion by August.
events.technicalChange: The round bought compute, international distribution, and product capacity.
events.meaning: Anthropic’s coding-first momentum translated into the fastest credible commercial challenge to OpenAI, reducing pressure to sell to Amazon or Google.
events.reaction: Investors rewarded execution; observers questioned whether multiple labs could sustain similar infrastructure burn.
events.lost: OpenAI’s enterprise narrative and smaller model vendors’ access to capital.

events.title: Kimi K2-Instruct-0905 improves context and agent stability
events.development: Moonshot refreshed K2’s instruction weights and hosted context.
events.technicalChange: Better coding, frontend generation, tool-call formatting, and longer context addressed weaknesses discovered after the initial open release without retraining the trillion-parameter base.
events.meaning: Frequent open-weight post-training updates became a competitive rhythm comparable to API vendors’ silent revisions.
events.reaction: The practical gains kept K2 relevant amid GPT-5 and Qwen3-Coder, though version fragmentation grew.
events.lost: fixed annual release cycles.

events.title: Qwen3-Next and Qwen3-Max split efficiency from scale
events.development: Alibaba released open 80B/3B-active Next models and a proprietary trillion-plus-parameter Max flagship.
events.technicalChange: Next interleaved Gated DeltaNet linear attention with standard attention, used ultra-sparse MoE and multi-token prediction, and delivered more than 10× long-context throughput; Max trained on 36T tokens for coding/agents and previewed deeper thinking.
events.meaning: Alibaba pursued two frontiers at once: radical open efficiency and maximum closed scale.
events.reaction: Next’s 3B active footprint drew technical enthusiasm; Max’s closed weights made claims harder to audit.
events.lost: dense attention’s default status and one-size-fits-all families.

events.title: GPT-5-Codex specializes one model for interactive and long-running work
events.development: OpenAI upgraded Codex across terminal, IDE, web, and GitHub with a coding-specialized GPT-5 variant.
events.technicalChange: Dynamic compute allocation let it respond quickly to small tasks or work independently for hours on refactors, code review, debugging, and tests; it adhered more closely to AGENTS.md instructions.
events.meaning: Coding-model design increasingly targeted the harness’s temporal rhythm rather than static code completion.
events.reaction: Developers reported major persistence gains; Claude Code remained the primary workflow rival.
events.lost: generic GPT-5 for difficult software tasks and independent IDE differentiation.

events.title: Grok 4 Fast compresses flagship reasoning into a cheap 2M-context model
events.development: xAI released one set of weights supporting reasoning and non-reasoning modes.
events.technicalChange: Long context, native web/X/code tools, and post-training efficiency delivered comparable search performance with a claimed 40% fewer thinking tokens and radically lower cost than Grok 4.
events.meaning: xAI shifted from benchmark-maximal Heavy compute toward price/performance and agent traffic.
events.reaction: Developers welcomed the cost drop; trust and safety concerns around Grok’s consumer behavior persisted.
events.lost: Grok 4’s price premium and smaller search-agent models.

events.title: Claude Sonnet 4.5 ships as California signs SB 53
events.development: Anthropic released a stronger coding/computer-use model and an Agent SDK; California enacted frontier-model transparency and serious-incident reporting requirements.
events.technicalChange: Sonnet improved long-horizon autonomous coding, computer interaction, and context management; the law required large developers to publish safety frameworks and report critical incidents while protecting whistleblowers.
events.meaning: Agent capability and enforceable safety process advanced together in the U.S. frontier industry’s home state.
events.reaction: Developers embraced Sonnet as a practical default; SB 53 was viewed as a narrower, more workable successor to vetoed SB 1047.
events.gained: Anthropic’s coding lead and California oversight.
events.lost: opaque frontier-safety practice.

events.title: GLM-4.6 extends context and coding performance
events.development: Zhipu upgraded its open flagship generation.
events.technicalChange: Context rose from 128K to 200K, with stronger code editing, reasoning, tool use, and more efficient token use for agents.
events.meaning: Zhipu matched the rapid open-model refresh cadence of Qwen and DeepSeek and strengthened its coding products.
events.reaction: The model gained usage through low-cost APIs and local hosts, though naming overlap with vision variants grew confusing.
events.lost: slower open release cycles.

events.title: AgentKit tries to make the whole agent lifecycle an OpenAI product
events.development: OpenAI launched visual Agent Builder, Connector Registry, ChatKit, datasets, trace grading, and prompt optimization.
events.technicalChange: Design, connectors, embedded UI, evaluation, deployment, and observability became one managed stack above Responses API.
events.meaning: OpenAI sought the control plane for enterprise agents, competing with cloud workflow tools and independent observability vendors.
events.reaction: No-code speed attracted enterprises; lock-in and overlap with the open Agents SDK drew criticism. OpenAI later announced the visual Builder/Evals products would wind down in 2026.
events.lost: fragmented agent tooling—then AgentKit itself lost momentum to code/skills-based workflows.

events.title: OpenAI and Broadcom announce custom AI accelerators
events.development: The companies said OpenAI-designed accelerators and Broadcom networking would begin deploying in racks in late 2026.
events.technicalChange: Custom XPUs co-designed for OpenAI workloads, high-bandwidth scale-up/out Ethernet, and rack-level systems aimed to internalize model–hardware optimization.
events.meaning: OpenAI sought leverage over NVIDIA cost and supply, while Broadcom graduated from Google/Meta custom silicon and networking into a visible frontier-lab partnership.
events.reaction: The scale impressed; circular financing, execution risk, and the continuing need for NVIDIA training clusters generated skepticism.
events.gained: OpenAI sovereignty and Broadcom’s XPU franchise.
events.lost: future NVIDIA share and Microsoft exclusivity.

events.title: Claude Haiku 4.5 brings near-frontier coding to the fast tier
events.development: Anthropic released a small, low-latency model with computer-use and agent capabilities.
events.technicalChange: It approached earlier Sonnet 4 coding at roughly one-third the cost and more than twice the speed, allowing multiple Haiku subagents to support a stronger coordinator.
events.meaning: Small models became active workers inside multi-agent systems rather than mere classifiers or routers.
events.reaction: Price/performance was well received; organizations still reserved complex planning for Sonnet/Opus.
events.gained: Anthropic’s volume tier and multi-agent economics.
events.lost: older Claude 3 Haiku and generic small models.

events.title: OpenAI completes its public-benefit recapitalization
events.development: The nonprofit became the OpenAI Foundation, continued controlling OpenAI Group PBC, and held conventional equity valued around $130 billion; Microsoft’s rights and ownership were reset.
events.technicalChange: Governance and capital structure—not a model—changed: investors gained normal equity upside while the foundation retained appointment/control powers and mission-focused safety authority.
events.meaning: OpenAI removed a major fundraising constraint without fully abandoning nonprofit control.
events.reaction: Supporters called it a pragmatic mission/capital balance; critics saw commercialization winning and questioned enforceability of public benefit.
events.gained: OpenAI’s ability to raise infrastructure capital, Microsoft liquidity, and the foundation’s paper wealth.
events.lost: the original capped-profit mechanism and some governance simplicity.

events.title: Kimi K2 Thinking targets long-horizon tool reasoning
events.development: Moonshot released a reasoning-tuned K2 variant.
events.technicalChange: The model could sustain long chains with web/code tools, repeatedly inspect observations, and revise plans, bringing the trillion-parameter MoE into the “thinking agent” category.
events.meaning: Kimi’s strategy evolved from long context to open agentic reasoning, intensifying Chinese competition with DeepSeek and Qwen.
events.reaction: Performance drew strong developer interest; very long traces and serving requirements made efficient harnesses essential.
events.lost: proprietary deep-research models’ scarcity.

events.title: GPT-5.1 and Codex-Max make reasoning adaptive and persistent
events.development: OpenAI released GPT-5.1 Instant/Thinking for ChatGPT and API, followed by GPT-5.1-Codex-Max.
events.technicalChange: Adaptive reasoning spent less compute on easy tasks, a no-reasoning mode cut latency, prompt caching extended, and native shell/apply-patch tools improved agent work. Codex-Max used compaction to continue across multiple context windows.
events.meaning: Long-running reliability depended on state compression and harness-native actions, not simply a larger window.
events.reaction: Users welcomed warmer chat and faster routine work; version churn continued to frustrate stable deployments.
events.lost: static reasoning budgets and single-window agents.

events.title: Grok 4.1 and 4.1 Fast improve personality and agent APIs
events.development: xAI upgraded the consumer model, then released a fast two-million-context API variant.
events.technicalChange: Preference post-training targeted emotional intelligence, style, lower hallucination, and creative collaboration; Fast added web/X/code/document and remote MCP tool endpoints.
events.meaning: xAI separated the social assistant’s personality from a low-cost agent backbone while using one real-time data advantage.
events.reaction: Blind preference tests improved, but safety and political-bias concerns stayed attached to the brand.
events.lost: earlier Grok 4 variants.

events.title: Gemini 3 Pro and Antigravity put agent workflows at Google’s center
events.development: Google previewed Gemini 3 Pro across the Gemini app, Search, API, Vertex, and a new agentic development environment; Deep Think followed for high-compute reasoning.
events.technicalChange: The model improved multimodal reasoning, coding, tool use, and visual UI generation; Antigravity let agents plan and operate editor, terminal, and browser while producing reviewable artifacts.
events.meaning: Google finally launched a frontier model into consumer, search, cloud, and agent products on day one.
events.reaction: The coordinated release was widely seen as a momentum turn; pricing and preview reliability remained concerns.
events.gained: Google’s integrated distribution and developer agent.
events.lost: OpenAI/Anthropic’s exclusive coding-agent narrative.

events.title: Claude Opus 4.5 strengthens long-running professional work
events.development: Anthropic replaced Opus 4.1 with a flagship for software engineering, computer use, research, and documents.
events.technicalChange: Better planning, context management, and self-correction improved multi-step agent reliability while token efficiency lowered the effective cost of difficult tasks.
events.meaning: Anthropic defended premium intelligence through execution quality rather than a new modality or extreme context headline.
events.reaction: Coding and enterprise users responded strongly; API price still reserved Opus for high-value work.
events.lost: Claude Opus 4.1 and GPT-5.1 in some coding workflows.

events.title: DeepSeek-V3.2 brings thinking into tool calls
events.development: DeepSeek released standard and high-compute “Speciale” variants.
events.technicalChange: Agent post-training across 1,800 environments and 85,000 complex instructions taught the model to reason while using tools, not before or after them; sparse attention improved long context.
events.meaning: DeepSeek answered closed agent models while maintaining open weights and aggressive pricing.
events.reaction: Speciale’s benchmark scores impressed, but high reasoning length and limited hosted access constrained everyday use.
events.lost: Western tool-reasoning exclusivity.

events.title: GLM-4.6V and GLM-4.7 unify visual agents and coding
events.development: Zhipu released a 106B multimodal model plus a free 9B Flash variant, then a stronger general/coding flagship.
events.technicalChange: GLM-4.6V offered native function calling from visual input and 128K multimodal context; GLM-4.7 improved reasoning, tool use, UI generation, and “vibe coding.”
events.meaning: Visual perception became an actionable tool-routing signal inside an open Chinese family.
events.reaction: Builders valued the 9B local option and coding gains; rapid numbering obscured which checkpoint fit which task.
events.lost: vision models without actions.

events.title: MCP moves to the Linux Foundation’s Agentic AI Foundation
events.development: Anthropic donated MCP to a foundation co-founded with Block and OpenAI, supported by Google, Microsoft, AWS, Cloudflare, and others; OpenAI contributed AGENTS.md and Block contributed goose.
events.technicalChange: Neutral governance, a registry, asynchronous/stateless protocol improvements, identity, extensions, and multi-language SDKs matured the standard.
events.meaning: Core agent interfaces became shared infrastructure rather than an Anthropic-controlled advantage.
events.reaction: The cross-industry coalition was treated as confirmation that MCP had won the connector standard race.
events.gained: Linux Foundation, open agent standards, tool developers.
events.lost: any single vendor’s control of agent interoperability.

events.title: GPT-5.2 and GPT-5.2-Codex target professional and persistent work
events.development: OpenAI released Instant, Thinking, Pro, then a coding-specialized variant.
events.technicalChange: Long-context reasoning, spreadsheets/presentations, tool use, vision, and long-running agents improved; Codex added compaction, large refactors/migrations, stronger Windows support, and defensive-cyber capability.
events.meaning: The product benchmark shifted from academic questions toward complete economic tasks and multi-hour repository change.
events.reaction: Enterprise evaluations improved, while users saw less dramatic conversational difference and continued release fatigue.
events.lost: GPT-5.1 and point document tools.

events.title: NVIDIA licenses Groq’s inference technology and hires its leaders
events.development: Groq entered a nonexclusive licensing agreement; founder Jonathan Ross, president Sunny Madra, and other staff joined NVIDIA while GroqCloud continued independently.
events.technicalChange: Compiler-scheduled LPU inference expertise could be integrated beside NVIDIA GPUs and software, especially for deterministic low-latency decode.
events.meaning: NVIDIA absorbed a credible architectural threat rather than waiting for it to scale, foreshadowing Groq LPUs inside the Rubin platform.
events.reaction: The reported deal value looked acquisition-like despite the nonexclusive form; customers questioned Groq’s independent roadmap.
events.gained: NVIDIA’s inference portfolio and Groq investors/team.
events.lost: Groq’s strategic independence and the alternative-hardware field’s strongest pure-play brand.

events.title: xAI raises $20 billion to scale Colossus and Grok
events.development: xAI closed an upsized Series E backed by financial investors plus NVIDIA and Cisco.
events.technicalChange: The financing supported Colossus I and II, which xAI said ended 2025 above one million H100-equivalent GPUs, and further reinforcement-learning compute for the Grok 4 line.
events.meaning: Compute procurement, real-time X distribution, consumer reach, and model training were being financed as one vertically integrated system.
events.reaction: The round confirmed xAI as a capital-scale frontier lab, although its self-reported compute and user figures were difficult to compare with audited rivals.
events.gained: xAI, NVIDIA, and large sovereign/financial backers.
events.lost: smaller labs unable to finance gigawatt-scale infrastructure.

events.title: Zhipu becomes the first major foundation-model pure play to list publicly
events.development: Knowledge Atlas Technology, the company behind Z.ai and GLM, listed in Hong Kong after raising about $552–558 million.
events.technicalChange: An IPO is not a model upgrade, but public capital gave an independent Chinese lab a new route to finance pretraining, inference subsidies, and domestic accelerator work.
events.meaning: Frontier-model economics became visible through a public company, and Hong Kong became a financing venue for China’s “AI tiger” cohort.
events.reaction: Shares finished the debut about 13% above the offer price, signaling appetite for the sector, while reporting emphasized Zhipu’s large losses relative to revenue.
events.gained: Zhipu, Hong Kong’s exchange, and investors seeking direct model exposure.
events.lost: private investors’ exclusive access and rivals still dependent on serial venture rounds.

events.title: Claude Cowork and a new constitution broaden Anthropic’s agent thesis
events.development: Anthropic previewed Cowork, a desktop agent derived from Claude Code, created Anthropic Labs to accelerate experimental products, and published a substantially rewritten Claude constitution.
events.technicalChange: Cowork applied filesystem access, tools, plans, and user review to general knowledge work; the constitution moved from a list of prohibitions toward reasoned principles, while remaining an input to training rather than a hard runtime rule.
events.meaning: Anthropic tried to transfer Claude Code’s execution loop to non-programmers without abandoning its safety-centered identity.
events.reaction: Claude Code’s reported billion-dollar run rate and MCP’s more than 100 million downloads made the expansion credible; desktop autonomy renewed concerns over permissions and accidental destructive actions.
events.gained: Anthropic’s product surface and constitutional-AI narrative.
events.lost: stand-alone desktop automation tools and Claude’s coding-only positioning.

events.title: OpenAI contracts 750 MW of Cerebras inference capacity
events.development: OpenAI and Cerebras announced a multi-year deployment of 750 megawatts of Cerebras systems through 2028.
events.technicalChange: Cerebras’s wafer-scale engines keep weights and bandwidth close to compute, targeting very high per-user token rates and low response latency rather than merely maximum batch throughput.
events.meaning: OpenAI diversified beyond GPU-only serving and made latency a first-class model-product variable.
events.reaction: The scale validated wafer-scale inference, while observers noted that delivery, power, and economics—not a demo benchmark—would determine the partnership’s impact.
events.lost: NVIDIA’s exclusivity at the inference layer, at least at the margin.

events.title: Qwen3-Max-Thinking makes tool use part of test-time scaling
events.development: Alibaba released the reasoning form of its largest proprietary Qwen3 model.
events.technicalChange: The model combined adaptive tool use with self-reflection, allowing it to decide when to search, execute code, or reconsider intermediate results during a longer reasoning trajectory.
events.meaning: China’s largest cloud vendor was no longer competing only through open checkpoints; it also had a premium, hosted reasoning tier.
events.reaction: Strong benchmark results drew attention, but the closed weights and high-compute inference made it a different proposition from Qwen’s popular open models.
events.lost: the idea that Qwen’s strategic leverage came only from open-weight distribution.

events.title: Kimi K2.5 and Agent Swarm parallelize multimodal work
events.development: Moonshot released Kimi K2.5, then previewed an agent-swarm mode.
events.technicalChange: K2.5 added native visual understanding to the K2 agent foundation; the swarm decomposed a job across concurrent subagents and synthesized their outputs instead of relying on one serial trajectory.
events.meaning: Parallel inference became a user-facing capability and a new way to spend test-time compute.
events.reaction: The demos made Moonshot look technically adventurous; cost, coordination errors, and reproducibility tempered enthusiasm for swarm benchmark gains.
events.lost: serial-only research assistants and labs without spare inference capacity.

events.title: Mistral Vibe, Small 4, and Forge sharpen Europe’s sovereign stack
events.development: Mistral upgraded its terminal coding agent, released Mistral Small 4 under Apache 2.0, and launched Forge for training enterprise-specific frontier models.
events.technicalChange: Vibe 2.0 added custom subagents, skills, clarification, and configurable permissions; Small 4 unified text/image input, coding, and selectable reasoning in a 119B-parameter MoE with about 6B active parameters and 256K context; Forge adapted models to proprietary organizational data.
events.meaning: Mistral’s strategy combined an efficient open worker, an agent harness, and private model-building rather than trying to outspend U.S. labs on one giant general model.
events.reaction: European and on-premises buyers welcomed the license and small active footprint; the flagship capability gap and requirement for multi-GPU serving still constrained mass local use.
events.gained: Mistral, sovereign-AI buyers, and European model autonomy.
events.lost: closed-only enterprise vendors and older Mistral specialist checkpoints consolidated by Small 4.

events.title: SpaceX acquires xAI
events.development: SpaceX announced that it had acquired xAI.
events.technicalChange: The transaction placed Grok, X-derived real-time data, Colossus data centers, satellite connectivity, launch capacity, and a proposed orbital-compute program under one corporate roof.
events.meaning: xAI’s resource base expanded from an AI/social platform to a space, communications, energy, and compute conglomerate.
events.reaction: Supporters saw an unmatched infrastructure flywheel; critics saw governance, valuation, and related-party risk concentrated around Elon Musk.
events.gained: the combined SpaceXAI capital and infrastructure stack.
events.lost: xAI’s stand-alone governance and rivals without captive communications or launch assets.

events.title: Codex becomes a multi-agent desktop, then gets GPT-5.3-Codex
events.development: OpenAI launched the Codex macOS app and three days later released GPT-5.3-Codex.
events.technicalChange: The app coordinated concurrent agents in isolated worktrees with reusable skills, automations, review, and sandboxing; the model improved long-running tool work and ran about 25% faster than its predecessor.
events.meaning: A coding harness became a persistent command center, and model/harness co-design became part of the product advantage.
events.reaction: Developers welcomed parallel work and artifact review, while asking how much autonomy could be trusted in real repositories; OpenAI classified the model at its first “High” cyber-capability threshold.
events.lost: single-agent editor extensions and generic chat-based coding.

events.title: Claude Opus 4.6 in Claude Code makes sustained delegation feel real
events.development: Anthropic released Opus 4.6 across Claude, Claude Code, and the API.
events.technicalChange: A one-million-token context window entered beta, alongside better long-horizon planning, coding, computer use, and context retention.
events.meaning: Anthropic answered Codex’s persistence with a premium model designed to stay coherent across very large projects.
events.reaction: Enterprise and coding users viewed it as a strong new ceiling; price and the operational difficulty of one-million-token prompts limited routine use.
events.lost: Opus 4.5 and smaller-context incumbents.
events.whyItFeltDifferent: In Claude Code, the improvement was not simply better autocomplete or a higher coding score. The model could inspect a substantial codebase, form and revise a plan, use tools, preserve intent through long runs, recover from errors, and return a coherent change for review. For many practitioners, the governing metaphor changed from pair-programming with a chatbot to managing an unusually fast junior-to-mid-level engineer—still fallible and in need of supervision, but capable of owning a meaningful unit of work.

events.title: GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark previews interactive coding above 1,000 tokens per second
events.development: OpenAI previewed a compact Codex variant on Cerebras hardware for ChatGPT Pro users.
events.technicalChange: Spark used a 128K text context and a latency-optimized stack that OpenAI reported could exceed 1,000 output tokens per second.
events.meaning: Coding split into at least two product modes: deep asynchronous agency and near-instant interactive iteration.
events.reaction: The speed felt qualitatively different, but restricted access, text-only input, and a smaller context made it a complement rather than a replacement.
events.gained: Cerebras and OpenAI’s real-time coding experience.
events.lost: GPU-serving stacks optimized only for aggregate throughput.

events.title: GLM-5 scales open agent reasoning on non-NVIDIA training hardware
events.development: Zhipu released GLM-5 under the MIT license.
events.technicalChange: The 744B-parameter mixture-of-experts model activated roughly 40B parameters per token, trained on 28.5T tokens, used DeepSeek Sparse Attention, and used the slime asynchronous reinforcement-learning system; Zhipu emphasized training on domestic accelerators.
events.meaning: A Chinese lab showed that frontier-scale open models and agent RL could advance despite U.S. access restrictions.
events.reaction: The scale and license impressed the open community; deployment remained demanding and benchmark claims needed independent replication.
events.gained: Zhipu, Chinese accelerator ecosystems, and open-model builders.
events.lost: export controls’ ability to freeze model progress and smaller local-deployment footprints.

events.title: Gemini 3 Deep Think and 3.1 Pro raise Google’s reasoning ceiling
events.development: Google upgraded its high-compute Deep Think mode, then introduced Gemini 3.1 Pro across the app, API, Vertex AI, and developer tools.
events.technicalChange: Deep Think used parallel reasoning for science, mathematics, and engineering; 3.1 Pro improved complex problem solving, coding, and multimodal understanding in the general flagship.
events.meaning: Google separated expensive deliberation from the broadly deployable frontier model while distributing both through its cloud and consumer surfaces.
events.reaction: Scientific and coding results were strong, though preview labels and shifting Gemini names still complicated procurement.
events.lost: labs without both a high-compute mode and mass distribution.

events.title: Anthropic raises $30 billion and makes Sonnet 4.6 the default Claude
events.development: Anthropic announced a $30 billion Series G at a $380 billion post-money valuation, then shipped Sonnet 4.6.
events.technicalChange: Sonnet brought a one-million-token beta window plus better coding, computer use, and agent planning to the mainstream price tier.
events.meaning: Claude’s most economically important model moved closer to the prior Opus frontier while Claude Code’s annualized revenue had reportedly passed $2.5 billion.
events.reaction: Investors endorsed Anthropic’s enterprise/coding momentum; the valuation magnified pressure to convert model leadership into durable margins.
events.gained: Anthropic’s balance sheet and high-volume tier.
events.lost: Sonnet 4.5, Opus-only workflows, and smaller enterprise challengers.

events.title: Qwen3.5 unifies vision, long context, and efficient open inference
events.development: Alibaba released an open-weight Qwen3.5 flagship.
events.technicalChange: The 397B-parameter mixture-of-experts model activated about 17B parameters, combined Gated DeltaNet with sparse attention, natively processed text and vision, supported 201 languages, and offered up to one million hosted tokens.
events.meaning: Open deployment no longer required choosing between multimodality, agent ability, or efficient activation.
events.reaction: Developers praised capability per active parameter and multilingual breadth; serving the full checkpoint still required serious infrastructure.
events.gained: Qwen’s open ecosystem and Alibaba Cloud.
events.lost: older dense open models and Western-only multilingual assumptions.

events.title: Taalas HC1 hardwires a model for ultra-fast inference
events.development: Taalas disclosed its first “hardcoded” model accelerator, manufactured on TSMC’s 6 nm process.
events.technicalChange: Instead of repeatedly fetching weights from external memory, HC1 embedded the model’s dataflow and weights into an 815 mm² chip; Taalas claimed roughly 17,000 Llama-3.1-8B tokens per second per user at about 2.5 kW.
events.meaning: Specialization challenged the assumption that every inference workload should run on a programmable GPU.
events.reaction: The speed/efficiency claim drew intense interest, but it was a vendor result for one small fixed model; flexibility, yield, and update economics were open questions.
events.lost: general-purpose accelerators on stable, very-high-volume models—if the economics held.

events.title: Google fills out Gemini’s low-cost, embedding, and compound-tool layers
events.development: Google released Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite, Gemini Embedding 2, and Gemini API tooling updates.
events.technicalChange: Flash-Lite targeted high-volume low-cost inference; Embedding 2 mapped text, images, video, audio, and documents into one vector space; the API could combine built-in and custom tools and circulate context more efficiently.
events.meaning: Google addressed the full retrieval-and-agent pipeline, not only flagship reasoning.
events.reaction: Developers welcomed a coherent stack and cheaper serving, while benchmark churn made cross-generation comparisons difficult.
events.gained: Google Cloud and end-to-end Gemini applications.
events.lost: point embedding vendors and orchestration glue built around one tool at a time.

events.title: GPT-5.4, mini, and nano make computer use a model-family capability
events.development: OpenAI launched GPT-5.4 Thinking/Pro, then GPT-5.4 mini and nano.
